text: Life is not a series of gig-lamps symmetrically arranged; life is a luminous halo, a semi-transparent envelope surrounding us from the beginning of consciousness to the end.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: The Common Reader (1925) · "Modern Fiction"

text: A whole lifetime was too short to bring out, the full flavour; to extract every ounce of pleasure, every shade of meaning.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: Mrs Dalloway (1925)

text: A light here required a shadow there.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: To the Lighthouse (1927) · Part I, Ch. 9

text: No need to hurry. No need to sparkle. No need to be anybody but oneself.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: A Room of One's Own (1929) · Ch. 1, p. 17

text: Lock up your libraries if you like; but there is no gate, no lock, no bolt that you can set upon the freedom of my mind.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: A Room of One's Own (1929) · Ch. 4, p. 90

text: Better was it to go unknown and leave behind you an arch, a potting shed, a wall where peaches ripen, than to burn like meteor and leave no dust.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: Orlando: A Biography (1928) · Ch. 2

text: Though we see the same world, we see it through different eyes. Any help we can give you must be different from that you can give yourselves, and perhaps the value of that help may lie in the fact of that difference.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: Three Guineas (1938) · Ch. 1, p. 18

text: Books are the mirrors of the soul.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: Between the Acts (1941)

text: Happiness is to have a little string onto which things will attach themselves.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: A Moment's Liberty (1990) · Monday 20 April 1925

text: Happily, at forty-six I still feel as experimental and on the verge of getting at the truth as ever.
author: Virginia Woolf
citation: A Moment's Liberty (1990) · Saturday 21 April, 1929

text: I had a very pleasant evening, however, though you will probably find out that there was no particular reason for it; but I do not think it worth while to wait for enjoyment until there is some real opportunity for it.
author: Jane Austen
work: Letters of Jane Austen — Brabourne Edition
citation: Letters · Letter (1799-01-21) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

text: The pleasures of friendship, of unreserved conversation, of similarity of taste and opinions will make good amends for orange wine.
author: Jane Austen
work: Letters of Jane Austen — Brabourne Edition
citation: Letters · Letter to Cassandra (1808-06-20) [Letters of Jane Austen -- Brabourne Edition]

text: There is nothing I would not do for those who are really my friends. I have no notion of loving people by halves, it is not my nature.
author: Jane Austen
citation: Letters · Northanger Abbey

text: One half of the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other.
author: Jane Austen
citation: Works · Emma (1815)

text: Ah! there is nothing like staying at home for real comfort.
author: Jane Austen
citation: Works · Emma (1815)

text: One does not love a place the less for having suffered in it, unless it has been all suffering, nothing but suffering.
author: Jane Austen
citation: Works · Persuasion (1817)

text: They say the first sentence in any speech is always the hardest. Well, that one’s behind me, anyway.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: The Poet and the World (1996)

text: Inspiration is not the exclusive privilege of poets or artists.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: The Poet and the World (1996)

text: Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous “I don’t know.”
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: The Poet and the World (1996)

text: Any knowledge that doesn’t lead to new questions quickly dies out: it fails to maintain the temperature required for sustaining life.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: The Poet and the World (1996)

text:
I’m working on the world,
revised, improved edition,
featuring fun for fools
blues for brooders,
combs for bald pates,
tricks for old dogs.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: Poems New and Collected (1998) · Calling Out to Yeti (1957) · I'm Working on the World"

text:
My apologies to the felled tree for the table’s four legs.
My apologies to great questions for small answers.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: Poems New and Collected (1998) · Could Have (1972) · "Under One Small Star"

text:
We call it a grain of sand
but it calls itself neither grain nor sand.
It does just fine without a name,
whether general, particular,
permanent, passing,
incorrect or apt.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: Poems New and Collected (1998) · The People on the Bridge (1986) · "View with a Grain of Sand"

text:
We’re extremely fortunate
not to know precisely
the kind of world we live in.
One would have
to live a long, long time,
unquestionably longer
than the world itself.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: Poems New and Collected (1998) · The End and the Beginning (1993) · "We're Extremely Fortunate"

text:
I’d have to be really quick
to describe clouds —
a split second’s enough
for them to start being something else. Their trademark:
they don’t repeat a single
shape, shade, pose, arrangement.
author: Wisława Szymborska
citation: Poems New and Collected (1998) · New Poems 1993–97 · "Clouds"

text: We have been troubled about the world, and had almost lost faith in man; it helps to think about the long history of the earth, and of how life came to be. And when we think in terms of millions of years, we are not so impatient that our own problems be solved tomorrow.

text: The sediments are a sort of epic poem of the earth.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sea Around Us (1951) · Chapter 6, Page 98

text: As human beings, we are part of the whole stream of life.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: Speech (1954)

text: Our origins are of the earth. And so there is in us a deeply seated response to the natural universe, which is part of our humanity.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: Speech (1954)

text: A preoccupation with the wonder and beauty of the earth has strongly influenced the course of my life.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: Speech (1954)

text: A child’s world is fresh and new and beautiful, full of wonder and excitement.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sense of Wonder (1965)

text: A rainy day is the perfect time for a walk in the woods.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sense of Wonder (1965)

text: Those who dwell, as scientists or laymen, among the beauties and mysteries of the earth are never alone or weary of life.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sense of Wonder (1965)

text: Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts.
author: Rachel Carson
citation: The Sense of Wonder (1965)

author: Charles Dickens
citation: Lucy's Song in The Village Coquettes (1836); later published in The Poems and Verses of Charles Dickens (1903)

text: To conceal anything from those to whom I am attached, is not in my nature. I can never close my lips where I have opened my heart.
author: Charles Dickens
citation: Master Humphrey's Clock, (1840) Vol. 1

text: Reflect upon your present blessings — of which every man has many — not on your past misfortunes, of which all men have some.
author: Charles Dickens
citation: Sketches by Boz (1836-1837) · Characters, Ch. 2: A Christmas Dinner

text: Suffering has been stronger than all other teaching, and has taught me to understand what your heart used to be. I have been bent and broken, but — I hope — into a better shape.
author: Charles Dickens
citation: Great Expectations (1860-1861) · Ch. 59

text:
What’s in a name? That which we call a rose,
By any other name would smell as sweet.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · Romeo and Juliet (1595) · Juliet, Act II, scene ii.

text: The course of true love never did run smooth.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · A Midsummer Night's Dream (1595) · Lysander, Act I, scene i.

text:
Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind,
And therefore is wing’d Cupid painted blind.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · A Midsummer Night's Dream (1595) · Helena, Act I, scene i.

text: As merry as the day is long.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · Much Ado About Nothing (1598) · Beatrice, Act II, scene i.

text:
All the world’s a stage,
And all the men and women merely players:
They have their exits and their entrances;
And one man in his time plays many parts.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · As You Like It (1599–1600) · Jaques, Act II, scene vii.

text: There is nothing either good or bad, but thinking makes it so.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · Hamlet (1600–1) · Hamlet, Act II, scene ii.

text: If music be the food of love, play on.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · Twelfth Night (1601) · Orsino, Act I, scene i.

text:
Come what come may,
Time and the hour runs through the roughest day.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · Macbeth (1606) · Macbeth, Act I, scene iii.

text:
We are such stuff
As dreams are made on; and our little life
Is rounded with a sleep.
author: William Shakespeare
citation: William Shakespeare Quotes · The Tempest (1611) · Prospero, Act IV, scene i.

text: When I get sick of what men do, I have only to walk a few steps in another direction to see what spiders do. Or what the weather does. This sustains me very well indeed.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to Carrie A. Wilson (1 May 1951)

text: If the world were merely seductive, that would be easy. If it were merely challenging, that would be no problem. But I arise in the morning torn between a desire to improve (or save) the world and a desire to enjoy (or savor) the world. This makes it hard to plan the day.
author: E. B. White
citation: Quoted in profile by Israel Shenker, "E. B. White: Notes and Comment by Author", The New York Times (11 July 1969)

text: Life’s meaning has always eluded me and I guess it always will. But I love it just the same.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to Mary Virginia Parrish (29 August 1969)

text: As long as there is one upright man, as long as there is one compassionate woman, the contagion may spread and the scene is not desolate. Hope is the one thing left to us in a bad time.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to M. Nadeau (30 March 1973)

text: Sailors have an expression about the weather: they say the weather is a great bluffer. I guess the same is true of our human society — things can look dark, then a break shows in the clouds, and all is changed.
author: E. B. White
citation: Letter to M. Nadeau (30 March 1973)

text: The future, wave or no wave, seems to me no unified dream but a mince pie, long in the baking, never quite done.
author: E. B. White
citation: One Man's Meat (1942) · A review of The Wave of the Future by Anne Morrow Lindbergh in Harpers Magazine (December 1940)

text: I am always humbled by the infinite ingenuity of the lord, who can make a red barn cast a blue shadow.
author: E. B. White
citation: One Man's Meat (1942) · A Winter Diary: January, 1941

text: Life is always a rich and steady time when you are waiting for something to happen or to hatch.
author: E. B. White
citation: Charlotte's Web (1952) · Ch. 22

text:
It is brave to be involved
To be not fearful to be unresolved.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: "do not be afraid of no" from Annie Allen (1949)

text:
Exhaust the little moment.
Soon it dies.
And be it gash or gold it will not come
Again in this identical guise.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: "exhaust the little moment" from Annie Allen (1949)

text: As you get older, you find that often the wheat, disentangling itself from the chaff, comes out to meet you.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Report From Part One (1972)

text:
To be in love
Is to touch with a lighter hand.
In yourself you stretch, you are well.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: "To Be In Love"

text:
I pass you my Poem! — to tell you
we are all vulnerable —
the midget, the Mighty,
the richest, the poor.
Men, women, children, and trees.
I am vulnerable.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text: My Poem is life, and not finished.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text:
Wherever life can grow, it will.
It will sprout out,
and do the best it can.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text: You don’t get all your questions answered in this world.
author: Gwendolyn Brooks
citation: Winnie (1988) · "Song of Winnie"

text: Nothing is more common than good things: the point in question is only to discriminate them; and it is certain that they are all natural and within our reach and even known to all mankind.
author: Blaise Pascal
citation: The Art of Persuasion

text: It is not among extraordinary and fantastic things that excellence is to be found, of whatever kind it may be. We rise to attain it and become removed from it: it is oftenest necessary to stoop for it.
author: Blaise Pascal
citation: The Art of Persuasion

text: The best books are those, which those who read them believe they themselves could have written.
author: Blaise Pascal
citation: The Art of Persuasion

text: Character, not circumstances, makes the man.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: "Democracy and Education", address at the Institute of Arts and Sciences, Brooklyn, New York (30 September 1896)

text: I think I have learned that the best way to lift one’s self up is to help someone else.
author: Booker T. Washington
work: The Story of My Life and Work
citation: The Story of My Life and Work, vol. I (1900), ch. XV: Cuban Education and the Chicago Peace Jubilee Address

text: There is no power on earth, that can neutralize the influence of a high, pure, simple and useful life.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: "The Virtue of Simplicity," from Character Building: Being Addresses Delivered on Sunday Evenings to the Students of Tuskegee Institute (1902), p. 41

text: There are two ways of exerting one’s strength: one is pushing down, the other is pulling up.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: As quoted in The Great Quotations (1971) edited by George Seldes, p. 366

text: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: 1900s · Up From Slavery (1901) · Chapter II: Boyhood Days

text: I learned the lesson that great men cultivate love, and that only little men cherish a spirit of hatred. I learned that assistance given to the weak makes the one who gives it strong; and that oppression of the unfortunate makes one weak.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: 1900s · Up From Slavery (1901) · Chapter XI: Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie On Them

text: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: 1900s · Up From Slavery (1901) · Chapter XI: Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie On Them. · This statement was quoted in Charm and Courtesy in Conversation (1904) by Frances Bennett Callaway, p. 153 as "I permit no man to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him." It has also often been paraphrased in various other ways:

text: Few things can help an individual more than to place responsibility on him, and to let him know that you trust him.
author: Booker T. Washington
citation: 1900s · Up From Slavery (1901) · Chapter XI: Making Their Beds Before They Could Lie On Them

text: In anything at all, perfection is finally attained not when there is no longer anything to add, but when there is no longer anything to take away, when a body has been stripped down to its nakedness.
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
citation: Terre des Hommes (1939) · Ch III : The Tool · It seems that perfection is attained not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing more to remove.

text: Transport of the mails, transport of the human voice, transport of flickering pictures — in this century, as in others, our highest accomplishments still have the single aim of bringing men together.
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
citation: Terre des Hommes (1939) · Ch III : The Tool

text: It is another of the miraculous things about mankind that there is no pain nor passion that does not radiate to the ends of the earth. Let a man in a garret but burn with enough intensity and he will set fire to the world.
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
citation: Terre des Hommes (1939) · Ch. IX Barcelona and Madrid (1936)

text: No man can draw a free breath who does not share with other men a common and disinterested ideal. Life has taught us that love does not consist in gazing at each other but in looking outward together in the same direction.
author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
citation: Terre des Hommes (1939) · Ch. IX Barcelona and Madrid (1936)

text: A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately at peace with himself. What a man can be, he must be.
author: Abraham Maslow
citation: 1940s · "A Theory of Human Motivation", in Psychological Review, vol. 50, no. 4 (1943), p. 382 · Also in Motivation and Personality (1954), p. 93 (see below)

text: This tendency might be phrased as the desire to become more and more what one is, to become everything that one is capable of becoming.
author: Abraham Maslow
citation: 1950s · Motivation and Personality (1954) · p. 93

text: Love, safety, belongingness and respect from other people are almost panaceas for the situational disturbances and even for some of the mild character disturbances.
author: Abraham Maslow
citation: 1950s · Motivation and Personality (1954) · p. 103

text: One of the goals of education should be to teach that life is precious.
author: Abraham Maslow
citation: 1950s · Motivation and Personality (1954) · p. 255

text: Education is learning to grow, learning what to grow toward, learning what is good and bad, learning what is desirable and undesirable, learning what to choose and what not to choose.
author: Abraham Maslow
work: The Farther Reaches of Human Nature
citation: 1970s · The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971)

text: There are years that ask questions and years that answer.
author: Zora Neale Hurston
citation: Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937) · Ch. 3, p. 21

text: Mama exhorted her children at every opportunity to “jump at de sun.” We might not land on the sun, but at least we would get off the ground.
author: Zora Neale Hurston
citation: Dust Tracks on a Road (1942) · Ch.2 : My Folks, p. 13

text: Love, I find is like singing. Everybody can do enough to satisfy themselves, though it may not impress the neighbors as being very much.
author: Zora Neale Hurston
citation: Dust Tracks on a Road (1942) · Ch. 14 : Love, p. 203

text: What a comfort one familiar face is in a howling wilderness of strangers!
author: L. M. Montgomery
citation: Anne of the Island (1915) · Ch. 3

text: Life had taught her to be brave, to be patient, to love, to forgive.
author: L. M. Montgomery
citation: Rainbow Valley (1919) · Ch. 13

text: It is never quite safe to think we have done with life. When we imagine we have finished our story fate has a trick of turning the page and showing us yet another chapter.
author: L. M. Montgomery
citation: Rainbow Valley (1919)

text: We miss so much out of life if we don’t love. The more we love the richer life is—even if it is only some little furry or feathery pet.
author: L. M. Montgomery
citation: Rainbow Valley (1919)

text: There is nothing in the world, I venture to say, that would so effectively help one to survive even the worst conditions, as the knowledge that there is a meaning in one’s life.
author: Viktor Frankl
citation: Man's Search for Meaning (1946; 1959; 1984) · p. 126 in the 1984 Pocket Books edition

text: Ultimately, man should not ask what the meaning of his life is, but rather must recognize that it is he who is asked. In a word, each man is questioned by life; and he can only answer to life by answering for his own life; to life he can only respond by being responsible.
author: Viktor Frankl
citation: Man's Search for Meaning (1946; 1959; 1984)

text: What man actually needs is not a tensionless state but rather the striving and struggling for some goal worthy of him. What he needs is not the discharge of tension at any cost, but the call of a potential meaning waiting to be fulfilled by him.
author: Viktor Frankl
citation: Man's Search for Meaning (1946; 1959; 1984)

text: There are no events but thoughts and the heart’s hard turning, the heart’s slow learning where to love and whom. The rest is merely gossip, and tales for other times.
author: Annie Dillard
citation: Holy the Firm (1977)

text: No claims of any and all revelations could be so far-fetched as a single giraffe.
author: Annie Dillard
citation: Pilgrim at Tinker Creek (1976) · chapter 8, "Intricacy", page 146

text: What is a weed? A plant whose virtues have yet to be discovered.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Fortune of the Republic (1878)

text: We are never without a pilot. When we know not how to steer, and dare not hoist a sail, we can drift. The current knows the way, though we do not. The ship of heaven guides itself, and will not accept a wooden rudder.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: "The Sovereignty of Ethics", in The North America Review, no. 262 (May–June 1878) p. 407

text: We are always getting ready to live, but never living.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Journals (1822–1863) · April 12, 1834

text: Do not be too timid and squeamish about your actions. All life is an experiment. The more experiments you make the better.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Journals (1822–1863) · November 11, 1842

text: The sky is the daily bread of the eyes.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: The stars awaken a certain reverence, because though always present, they are inaccessible; but all natural objects make a kindred impression, when the mind is open to their influence. Nature never wears a mean appearance.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Nature (1836) · Nature

text: Give me health and a day, and I will make the pomp of emperors ridiculous.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Nature (1836) · Beauty

text: Explore, and explore, and explore. Be neither chided nor flattered out of your position of perpetual inquiry. Neither dogmatise yourself, nor accept another’s dogmatism.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Literary Ethics (1838)

text:
But all sorts of things and weather
Must be taken in together
To make up a year,
And a sphere.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Poems (1847) · Fable

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Poems (1847) · Fable

text:
Rhodora! if the sages ask thee why
This charm is wasted on the earth and sky,
Tell them, dear, that, if eyes were made for seeing,
Then beauty is its own excuse for Being.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Poems (1847) · The Rhodora

text:
Go where he will, the wise man is at home,
His hearth the earth, his hall the azure dome.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Poems (1847) · Wood-notes, st. 3

text: Keep cool: it will be all one a hundred years hence.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Representative Men (1850) · Montaigne; or, The Skeptic

text: The thing done avails, and not what is said about it. An original sentence, a step forward, is worth more than all the censures.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: English Traits (1856) · First Visit to England

text: All the great speakers were bad speakers at first.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Conduct of Life (1860) · Power

text: You can never do a kindness too soon, for you never know how soon it will be too late.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Conduct of Life (1860) · Culture

text: I wish that life should not be cheap, but sacred. I wish the days to be as centuries, loaded, fragrant.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Conduct of Life (1860) · Considerations by the Way

text: Our chief want in life is somebody who shall make us do what we can.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Conduct of Life (1860) · Considerations by the Way

text: Make yourself necessary to somebody. Do not make life hard to any.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Conduct of Life (1860) · Considerations by the Way

text: All is riddle, and the key to a riddle is another riddle.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Conduct of Life (1860) · Illusions

text:
O tenderly the haughty day
Fills his blue urn with fire;
One morn is in the mighty heaven,
And one in our desire.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: May-Day and Other Pieces (1867) · Ode, st. 1

text:
The music that can deepest reach,
And cure all ill, is cordial speech.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: May-Day and Other Pieces (1867) · Merlin's Song, II

text:
Some of your hurts you have cured,
And the sharpest you still have survived,
But what torments of grief you endured
From evils which never arrived!
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: May-Day and Other Pieces (1867) · Borrowing From the French

text: The ornament of a house is the friends who frequent it.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Society and Solitude (1870) · Domestic Life

text: Write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Society and Solitude (1870) · Works and Days

text: Men love to wonder, and that is the seed of our science.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Society and Solitude (1870) · Works and Days; sometimes misquoted as "Men love to wonder, and that is the seed of science."

text: Don’t waste yourself in rejection, nor bark against the bad, but chant the beauty of the good.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Society and Solitude (1870) · Success

text: Hitch your wagon to a star.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Society and Solitude (1870) · Civilization

text: Nature paints the best part of a picture, carves the best parts of the statue, builds the best part of the house, and speaks the best part of the oration.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Society and Solitude (1870) · Art

text: The imagination is not a talent of some men but is the health of every man.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Letters and Social Aims (1876) · Poetry and Imagination

text: Life is not so short but that there is always time enough for courtesy.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Letters and Social Aims (1876) · Social Aims

text: Shall I tell you the secret of the true scholar? It is this: Every man I meet is my master at some point, and in that, I learn of him.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Letters and Social Aims (1876) · Greatness

text: In the highest civilization, the book is still the highest delight. He who has once known its satisfactions is provided with a resource against calamity.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Letters and Social Aims (1876) · Quotation and Originality

text: Each man is a hero and an oracle to somebody.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Letters and Social Aims (1876) · Quotation and Originality

text: We cannot overstate our debt to the Past, but the moment has the supreme claim.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: Letters and Social Aims (1876) · Quotation and Originality

text: Every man is a new method.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Natural History of Intellect, and Other Papers (1893) · "The Natural History of Intellect", p. 28

text: What strength belongs to every plant and animal in nature. The tree or the brook has no duplicity, no pretentiousness, no show. It is, with all its might and main, what it is, and makes one and the same impression and effect at all times.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
citation: The Natural History of Intellect, and Other Papers (1893) · "The Natural History of Intellect", p. 46

text: The whole difference between construction and creation is exactly this: that a thing constructed can only be loved after it is constructed; but a thing created is loved before it exists, as the mother can love the unborn child.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: Appreciations and Criticisms of the Works of Charles Dickens (1911) Ch. 2: "Pickwick Papers"

text: I would maintain that thanks are the highest form of thought; and that gratitude is happiness doubled by wonder.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: A Short History of England (1917), p. 59

text: I do not believe in a fate that falls on men however they act; but I do believe in a fate that falls on them unless they act.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: In The Illustrated London News (29 April 1922) · Collected in Generally Speaking (1929) "XX. On Holland"

text: There runs a strange law through the length of human history — that men are continually tending to undervalue their environment, to undervalue their happiness, to undervalue themselves.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: The Defendant (1901) · "Introduction"

text: It is a strange thing that many truly spiritual men, such as General Gordon, have actually spent some hours in speculating upon the precise location of the Garden of Eden. Most probably we are in Eden still. It is only our eyes that have changed.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: The Defendant (1901) · "Introduction"

text: I have investigated the dust-heaps of humanity, and found a treasure in all of them. I have found that humanity is not incidentally engaged, but eternally and systematically engaged, in throwing gold into the gutter and diamonds into the sea.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: The Defendant (1901) · "Introduction"

text: There is a road from the eye to the heart that does not go through the intellect. Men do not quarrel about the meaning of sunsets; they never dispute that the hawthorn says the best and wittiest thing about the spring.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: The Defendant (1901) · "A Defence of Heraldry"

text: The most unfathomable schools and sages have never attained to the gravity which dwells in the eyes of a baby of three months old. It is the gravity of astonishment at the universe, and astonishment at the universe is not mysticism, but a transcendent common-sense.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: The Defendant (1901) · "A Defence of Baby-Worship"

text: There is no such thing on earth as an uninteresting subject; the only thing that can exist is an uninterested person.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: Heretics (1905)

text: There is a great man who makes every man feel small. But the real great man is the man who makes every man feel great.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: Charles Dickens (1906) · Ch 1: "The Dickens Period"

text: These higher optimists, of whom Dickens was one, do not approve of the universe; they do not even admire the universe; they fall in love with it. They embrace life too close to criticize or even to see it.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: Charles Dickens (1906) · Ch 2: "The Boyhood of Dickens"

text: It is so easy to be solemn; it is so hard to be frivolous.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: All Things Considered (1908) · "The Case for the Ephemeral"

text: An inconvenience is only an adventure wrongly considered; an adventure is an inconvenience rightly considered.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: All Things Considered (1908) · "On Running After One's Hat"

text: It is not only possible to say a great deal in praise of play; it is really possible to say the highest things in praise of it. It might reasonably be maintained that the true object of all human life is play. Earth is a task garden; heaven is a playground.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: All Things Considered (1908) · "Oxford from Without"

text: The world will never starve for want of wonders; but only for want of wonder.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: Tremendous Trifles (1909) · Ch. I: "Tremendous Trifles"

text: The whole object of travel is not to set foot on foreign land; it is at last to set foot on one’s own country as a foreign land.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: Tremendous Trifles (1909) · Ch. XXXI: "The Riddle of the Ivy"

text: Poets have been mysteriously silent on the subject of cheese.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: Alarms and Discursions (1910) · 'Cheese,' p. 70

text: If a thing is worth doing, it is worth doing badly.
author: G. K. Chesterton
citation: What's Wrong With The World (1910) · Folly and Female Education

text: We are kept all as securely in Love in woe as in weal, by the Goodness of God.
author: Julian of Norwich
citation: Revelations of Divine Love (c. 1393) · Chapter 1

text: I may make all thing well, I can make all thing well, I will make all thing well, and I shall make all thing well; and thou shalt see thyself that all manner of thing shall be well.
author: Julian of Norwich
citation: The Thirteenth Revelation · Chapter 31

text: Let us not underrate the value of a fact; it will one day flower in a truth.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: "Natural History of Massachusetts". The Dial (July 1842) p. 39

text: It is not enough to be industrious; so are the ants. What are you industrious about?
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Letter to Harrison Blake (November 16, 1857)

text: Have no mean hours, but be grateful for every hour, and accept what it brings. The reality will make any sincere record respectable.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · July 6, 1840

text: Who looks in the sun will see no light else; but also he will see no shadow. Our life revolves unceasingly, but the centre is ever the same, and the wise will regard only the seasons of the soul.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · March 10, 1841

text: It is a great art to saunter.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · April 26, 1841

text: A slight sound at evening lifts me up by the ears, and makes life seem inexpressibly serene and grand. It may be Uranus, or it may be in the shutter.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: One cannot too soon forget his errors and misdemeanors. To dwell long upon them is to add to the offense. Repentance and sorrow can only be displaced by something better, which is as free and original as if they had not been.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · January 9, 1842

text: How vain it is to sit down to write when you have not stood up to live.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · August 19, 1851

text: The bluebird carries the sky on his back.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · April 3, 1852

text: Nature is full of genius, full of the divinity; so that not a snowflake escapes its fashioning hand.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · January 5, 1856

text: That man is the richest whose pleasures are the cheapest.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · March 11, 1856

text: You must love the crust of the earth on which you dwell more than the sweet crust of any bread or cake; you must be able to extract nutriment out of a sand heap.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Journals (1838-1859) · January 25, 1858

text: I came into this world, not chiefly to make this a good place to live in, but to live in it, be it good or bad.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Civil Disobedience (1849)

text: Gradually the village murmur subsided, and we seemed to be embarked on the placid current of our dreams, floating from past to future as silently as one awakes to fresh morning or evening thoughts.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849) · Saturday

text: The finest workers in stone are not copper or steel tools, but the gentle touches of air and water working at their leisure with a liberal allowance of time.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849) · Wednesday

text: It takes two to speak the truth, — one to speak, and another to hear.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849) · Wednesday

text: This world is but canvas to our imaginations.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849) · Wednesday

text:
My life has been the poem I would have writ,
But I could not both live and utter it.
author: Henry David Thoreau
work: My Life Has Been a Poem I Would Have Writ
citation: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (1849) · Friday · My Life Has Been a Poem I Would Have Writ

text: Why should we be in such desperate haste to succeed, and in such desperate enterprises? If a man does not keep pace with his companions, perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer. Let him step to the music which he hears, however measured or far away.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Money is not required to buy one necessity of the soul.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Only that day dawns to which we are awake. There is more day to dawn. The sun is but a morning star.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Life consists with wildness. The most alive is the wildest. Not yet subdued to man, its presence refreshes him.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Walking (June 1862)

text: The greatest compliment that was ever paid me was when one asked me what I thought, and attended to my answer. I am surprised, as well as delighted, when this happens, it is such a rare use he would make of me, as if he were acquainted with the tool.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Life Without Principle (1863) · p. 484

text: You must get your living by loving.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Life Without Principle (1863) · pp. 486–7

text: It requires more than a day’s devotion to know and to possess the wealth of a day.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Life Without Principle (1863) · p. 491

text: Why should we not meet, not always as dyspeptics, to tell our bad dreams, but sometimes as eupeptics, to congratulate each other on the ever glorious morning? I do not make an exorbitant demand, surely.
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: Life Without Principle (1863) · p. 495

text: Who could believe in prophecies of Daniel or of Miller that the world would end this summer, while one milkweed with faith matured its seeds?
author: Henry David Thoreau
citation: The Dispersion of Seeds (1993)

text: To know what you prefer, instead of humbly saying Amen to what the world tells you you ought to prefer, is to have kept your soul alive.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: An Inland Voyage (1878), Ch. III, "The Royal Sport Nautique".

text: Quiet minds cannot be perplexed or frightened but go on in fortune or misfortune at their own private pace, like a clock during a thunderstorm.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: 'La Fère of Cursed Memory', 15th vignette of An Inland Voyage (1878), in Collected Memoirs, Travel Sketches and Island Literature of Robert Louis Stevenson, Stevenson, e-artnow (2015)

text: For my part, I travel not to go anywhere, but to go. I travel for travel’s sake. The great affair is to move.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
work: Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes
citation: Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes (1878).

text: For there is a fellowship more quiet even than solitude, and which, rightly understood, is solitude made perfect.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
work: Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes
citation: Travels with a Donkey in the Cévennes (1878).

text: To be what we are, and to become what we are capable of becoming, is the only end of life.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
work: Familiar Studies of Men and Books
citation: Familiar Studies of Men and Books (1882).

text: In every part and corner of our life, to lose oneself is to be a gainer; to forget oneself is to be happy.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Old Mortality (1884).

text: So long as we love we serve; so long as we are loved by others, I would almost say that we are indispensable; and no man is useless while he has a friend.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: "Lay Morals" Ch. 4, in Lay Morals and Other Essays (1911).

text: Give us grace and strength to forbear and to persevere. Give us courage and gaiety and the quiet mind, spare to us our friends, soften to us our enemies.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Prayer, inscribed on the bronze memorial to Stevenson in St. Giles Cathedral, Edinburgh, Scotland

text: Our business in this world is not to succeed, but to continue to fail, in good spirits.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Complete Works, vol. 26, Reflections and Remarks on Human Life, section 4.

text: A good conscience is eight parts of courage.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Catriona, ch. XI (1893).

text: All who have meant good work with their whole hearts, have done good work, although they may die before they have the time to sign it. Every heart that has beat strong and cheerfully has left a hopeful impulse behind it in the world, and bettered the tradition of mankind.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Aes Triplex (1878) · 316.

text: You could read Kant by yourself, if you wanted; but you must share a joke with someone else.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers (1881) · Virginibus Puerisque, Ch. 1. · Cornhill Magazine, (August 1876)

text: Falling in love is the one illogical adventure, the one thing of which we are tempted to think as supernatural, in our trite and reasonable world.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers (1881) · Virginibus Puerisque, Ch. 3.

text: The true wisdom is to be always seasonable, and to change with a good grace in changing circumstances.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers (1881) · Crabbed Age and Youth.

text: There is no duty we so much underrate as the duty of being happy.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers (1881) · An Apology for Idlers.

text: A happy man or woman is a better thing to find than a five-pound note.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers (1881) · An Apology for Idlers.

text: To travel hopefully is a better thing than to arrive.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Virginibus Puerisque and Other Papers (1881) · El Dorado.

text: Though the coming of the day is still the most inspiriting, yet day’s departure, also, and the return of night refresh, renew, and quiet us; and in the pastures of the dusk we stand, like cattle, exulting in the absence of the load.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: The Silverado Squatters (1883) · Toils And Pleasures.

text:
The world is so full of a number of things,
I’m sure we should all be as happy as kings.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: A Child's Garden of Verses (1885) · Happy Thought.

text:
Go, little book, and wish to all
Flowers in the garden, meat in the hall,
A bin of wine, a spice of wit,
A house with lawns enclosing it,
A living river by the door,
A nightingale in the sycamore!
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Underwoods (1887) · Bk. I, Envoy · :Cf. Chaucer, Troilus and Cressida, bk. V, l. 1786

text: Gentleness and cheerfulness, these come before all morality; they are the perfect duties.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Across the Plains (1892) · Ch. XII, A Christmas Sermon.

text:
Wealth I ask not, hope nor love,
Nor a friend to know me;
All I ask, the heaven above
And the road below me.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Songs of Travel and Other Verses (1896) · No. I, The Vagabond, st. 4.

text:
I will make you brooches and toys for your delight
Of bird-song at morning and star-shine at night.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Songs of Travel and Other Verses (1896) · No. XI, Romance, st. 1.

text:
Bright is the ring of words
When the right man rings them.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
work: Songs of Travel and Other Verses
citation: Songs of Travel and Other Verses (1896) · No. XIV

text: The world was not made for us; it was made for ten hundred millions of men, all different from each other and from us; there’s no royal road there, we just have to sclamber and tumble.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Weir of Hermiston (1896) · Ch. 4, Opinions of the Bench.

text: The commonplaces are the great poetic truths.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
citation: Weir of Hermiston (1896) · Ch. 6, A Leaf from Christina's Psalm-book.

text: A very great deal more truth can become known than can be proven.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: "The Development of the Space-Time View of Quantum Electrodynamics," Nobel Lecture (11 December 1965)

text: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: "Cargo Cult Science", adapted from a 1974 Caltech commencement address; also published in Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!, p. 343

text: The imagination of nature is far, far greater than the imagination of man.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Value of Science (1955)

text: We are at the very beginning of time for the human race. It is not unreasonable that we grapple with problems. But there are tens of thousands of years in the future. Our responsibility is to do what we can, learn what we can, improve the solutions, and pass them on.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Value of Science (1955)

text: Nature uses only the longest threads to weave her patterns, so each small piece of her fabric reveals the organization of the entire tapestry.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Character of Physical Law (1965) · chapter 1, “The Law of Gravitation,” p. 34

text: Our imagination is stretched to the utmost, not, as in fiction, to imagine things which are not really there, but just to comprehend those things which are there.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Character of Physical Law (1965) · chapter 6, “Probability and Uncertainty — the Quantum Mechanical View of Nature,” p. 127-128

text: It is not unscientific to make a guess, although many people who are not in science think it is.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Character of Physical Law (1965) · chapter 7, “Seeking New Laws,” p. 165-166: video

text: I wanted very much to learn to draw, for a reason that I kept to myself: I wanted to convey an emotion I have about the beauty of the world.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985) · Part 5: "The World of One Physicist", "But Is It Art?", p. 261

text: There are all kinds of interesting questions that come from a knowledge of science, which only adds to the excitement and mystery and awe of a flower. It only adds. I don’t understand how it subtracts.
author: Richard Feynman
work: What Do You Care What Other People Think?
citation: What Do You Care What Other People Think? (1988) · "The Making of a Scientist," p. 11: video

text: I learned very early the difference between knowing the name of something and knowing something.
author: Richard Feynman
work: What Do You Care What Other People Think?
citation: What Do You Care What Other People Think? (1988) · "The Making of a Scientist," p. 14

text: Some people say, “How can you live without knowing?” I do not know what they mean. I always live without knowing. That is easy. How you get to know is what I want to know.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Meaning of It All (1999) · lecture I: "The Uncertainty of Science"

text: It is in the admission of ignorance and the admission of uncertainty that there is a hope for the continuous motion of human beings in some direction that doesn’t get confined, permanently blocked, as it has so many times before in various periods in the history of man.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Meaning of It All (1999) · lecture II: "The Uncertainty of Values"

text: The fact that you are not sure means that it is possible that there is another way someday.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Meaning of It All (1999) · lecture II: "The Uncertainty of Values"

text: I don’t know anything, but I do know that everything is interesting if you go into it deeply enough.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: The Pleasure of Finding Things Out (1999) · From Omni interview, "The Smartest Man in the World" (1979) p. 203

text: Do not read so much, look about you and think of what you see there.
author: Richard Feynman
citation: Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track (2005) · From a letter to Ashok Arora of Uttar Pradesh, India, dated 4 January 1967

text:
My soul is awakened, my spirit is soaring
And carried aloft on the wings of the breeze;
For above and around me the wild wind is roaring,
Arousing to rapture the earth and the seas.
author: Anne Brontë
work: Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell
citation: Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell (1846) · Lines Composed in a Wood on a Windy Day (1842)

text: If you would have your son to walk honourably through the world, you must not attempt to clear the stones from his path, but teach him to walk firmly over them — not insist upon leading him by the hand, but let him learn to go alone.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. III : A Controversy; Gilbert to Helen

text: A light wind swept over the corn; and all nature laughed in the sunshine.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. XV : An Encounter and its Consequences; Gilbert Markham

text: Smiles and tears are so alike with me, they are neither of them confined to any particular feelings: I often cry when I am happy, and smile when I am sad.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. XV : An Encounter and its Consequences; Gilbert Markham

text: What the world stigmatizes as romantic, is often more nearly allied to the truth than is commonly supposed; for, if the generous ideas of youth are too often over-clouded by the sordid views of after-life, that scarcely proves them to be false.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. XXXII : Comparisons: Information Rejected; Helen to Milicent

text: How odd it is that we so often weep for each other’s distresses, when we shed not a tear for our own!
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. XXXII : Comparisons: Information Rejected; Helen

text: No generous mind delights to oppress the weak, but rather to cherish and protect.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. XXXII : Comparisons: Information Rejected; Helen to Ralph

text: It is never too late to reform, as long as you have the sense to desire it, and the strength to execute your purpose.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. XLII : A Reformation; Helen to Ralph

text: There’s nothing like active employment to console the afflicted.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Tenant of Wildfell Hall (1848) · Ch. XLVII : Startling Intelligence; Eliza to Gilbert

text:
On all her breezes borne
Earth yields no scents like those;
But he, that dares not grasp the thorn
Should never crave the rose.
author: Anne Brontë
citation: The Narrow Way (1848)

text: Human relations are like the irregular verbs in a number of languages where nearly all verbs are irregular.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
citation: 1830s · The Journals of Søren Kierkegaard, 1830s · Journals A 126 (March 1836)

text: Most men pursue pleasure with such breathless haste that they hurry past it.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
citation: 1840s · Either/Or (1843) · Swenson, 1959, p. 28

text: Take a book, the poorest one written, but read it with the passion that it is the only book you will read-ultimately you will read everything out of it, that is, as much as there was in yourself, and you could never get more out of reading, even if you read the best of books.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
citation: 1840s · Stages on Life's Way (1845) · Stages on Life's Way, 1845 p. 363-364

text:
Happy the man whose wish and care
A few paternal acres bound,
Content to breathe his native air
In his own ground.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: "Ode on Solitude" (c. 1700), st. 1

text:
A little Learning is a dang’rous Thing;
Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian Spring:
There shallow Draughts intoxicate the Brain,
And drinking largely sobers us again.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: "An Essay on Criticism" (1709)

text: How vast a memory has Love!
author: Alexander Pope
citation: "Sappho to Phaon", line 52 (1712)

text:
For he lives twice who can at once employ
The present well, and e’en the past enjoy.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: Imitation of Martial, reported in Mr. Pope's Literary Correspondence (1737), Vol. V, p. 232; The Poems of Alexander Pope, ed. John Butt, sixth edition (Yale University Press, 1970), p. 117. Compare: "Ampliat ætatis spatium sibi vir bonus; hoc est Vivere bis vita posse priore frui" (Translated: "The good man prolongs his life; to be able to enjoy one's past life is to live twice"), Martial, X, 237.; "Thus would I double my life's fading space; For he that runs it well, runs twice his race", Abraham Cowley, Discourse XI, Of Myself, stanza xi.

text:
True ease in writing comes from art, not chance,
As those move easiest who have learn’d to dance.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: An Essay on Criticism (1711)

text: To err is human, to forgive divine.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: An Essay on Criticism (1711)

text:
Not chaos-like together crush’d and bruis’d,
But as the world, harmoniously confus’d,
Where order in variety we see,
And where, though all things differ, all agree.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: Windsor Forest (1713) · Line 13

text: A man should never be ashamed to own he has been in the wrong, which is but saying, in other words, that he is wiser today than he was yesterday.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: Thoughts on Various Subjects (1727)

text: To be angry, is to revenge the fault of others upon ourselves.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: Thoughts on Various Subjects (1727)

text:
Teach me to feel another’s woe,
To right the fault I see;
That mercy I to others show,
That mercy show to me.
author: Alexander Pope
citation: The Universal Prayer (1738) · Stanza 10; this extends upon the theme evident in the lines of Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene (1596), Book V, Canto ii, Stanza 42: "Who will not mercie unto others show, How can he mercy ever hope to have?"

text: Just because we don’t understand doesn’t mean that the explanation doesn’t exist.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: A Wrinkle in Time (1962)

text: You’re given the form, but you have to write the sonnet yourself. What you say is completely up to you.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: A Wrinkle in Time (1962)

text: The concentration of a small child at play is analogous to the concentration of the artist of any discipline. In real play, which is real concentration, the child is not only outside time, he is outside himself.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 1.3

text: We do have to use our minds as far as they will take us, yet acknowledging that they cannot take us all the way.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 1.10

text: A self is not something static, tied up in a pretty parcel and handed to the child, finished and complete. A self is always becoming.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 1.10

text: Love can’t be pinned down by a definition, and it certainly can’t be proved, anymore than anything else important in life can be proved.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 1.16

text: Nothing important is completely explicable.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 3.9

text: I wish that we worried more about asking the right questions instead of being so hung up on finding answers.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Crosswicks Journal · A Circle of Quiet (1972) · Section 4.8

text: When we were children, we used to think that when we were grown-up we would no longer be vulnerable. But to grow up is to accept vulnerability.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: Walking on Water (1980)

text: We are not to retreat from life, pinning our hopes on ‘elsewhere.’ but to know that we will come to that final destination best by living full here and now, be it through joy, or pain, or a mix of both.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: The Rock that Is Higher (1993)

text: There’s more to life than just the things that can be explained by encyclopedias and facts. Facts alone are not adequate.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: Penguins and Golden Calves (2003)

text: You can’t be a writer if you’re not a reader. It’s the great writers who teach us how to write. The third thing is to write. Just write a little bit every day. Even if it’s for only half an hour — write, write, write.
author: Madeleine L'Engle
citation: Penguins and Golden Calves (2003)

text: We are just an advanced breed of monkeys on a minor planet of a very average star. But we can understand the Universe. That makes us something very special.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: Der Spiegel (17 October 1988)

text: Mankind’s greatest achievements have come about by talking, and its greatest failures by not talking.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: British Telecom advertisement (1993), part of which was used in Pink Floyd's Keep Talking (1994) and Talkin' Hawkin' (2014)

text: Life would be tragic if it weren’t funny.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: As quoted in "The Science of Second-Guessing", The New York Times (12 December 2004)

text: My expectations were reduced to zero when I was 21. Everything since then has been a bonus.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: As quoted in "The Science of Second-Guessing", The New York Times (12 December 2004) · Unsourced variant: "When one's expectations are reduced to zero, one really appreciates everything one does have."

text: It is a waste of time to be angry about my disability. One has to get on with life and I haven’t done badly. People won’t have time for you if you are always angry or complaining.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: As quoted in "Return of the time lord" in The Guardian (27 September 2005)

text: Black holes ain’t as black as they are painted. They are not the eternal prisons they were once thought. Things can get out of a black hole, both to the outside, and possibly to another universe. So if you feel you are in a black hole, don’t give up. There’s a way out.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: Reith Lecture 2 : Black holes ain’t as black as they are painted (2015) · BBC Radio 4 audio file

text: I have noticed that even people who claim everything is predetermined and that we can do nothing to change it, look before they cross the road.
author: Stephen Hawking
work: Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays
citation: Black Holes and Baby Universes and Other Essays (1993) · pp. 133–135.

text: So next time someone complains that you have made a mistake, tell him that may be a good thing. Because without imperfection, neither you nor I would exist.
author: Stephen Hawking
work: Into The Universe with Stephen Hawking
citation: Into The Universe with Stephen Hawking (2010)

text: We are all different — but we share the same human spirit. Perhaps it’s human nature that we adapt — and survive.
author: Stephen Hawking
citation: Hawking (2013) · Official Trailer

text: One cannot be deeply responsive to the world without being saddened very often.
author: Erich Fromm
citation: ABC TV (25 May 1958)

text: The quest for certainty blocks the search for meaning. Uncertainty is the very condition to impel man to unfold his powers.
author: Erich Fromm
citation: Man for Himself (1947) · Ch. 3

text: Man’s main task in life is to give birth to himself, to become what he potentially is. The most important product of his effort is his own personality.
author: Erich Fromm
citation: Man for Himself (1947) · Ch. 4 "Problems of Humanistic Ethics"

text: Only the person who has faith in himself is able to be faithful to others.
author: Erich Fromm
citation: Man for Himself (1947) · Ch. 4

text: Envy, jealousy, ambition, any kind of greed are passions; love is an action, the practice of human power, which can be practiced only in freedom and never as a result of compulsion.
author: Erich Fromm
citation: The Art of Loving (1956)

text: Immature love says: “I love you because I need you.” Mature love says: “I need you because I love you.”
author: Erich Fromm
citation: The Art of Loving (1956) · Ch. 2

text: All men are in need of help and depend on one another. Human solidarity is the necessary condition for the unfolding of any one individual.
author: Erich Fromm
citation: The Art of Loving (1956) · Ch. 2

text: To hope means to be ready at every moment for that which is not yet born, and yet not become desperate if there is no birth in our lifetime.
author: Erich Fromm
citation: The Revolution of Hope: Toward a Humanized Technology (1968)

text: Until he extends the circle of his compassion to all living things, man will not himself find peace.
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: Kulturphilosophie (1923) · Variant translation: Until we extend the circle of compassion to all living things, we will not ourselves find peace.

text: True philosophy must start from the most immediate and comprehensive fact of consciousness: “I am life that wants to live, in the midst of life that wants to live.”
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: Kulturphilosophie (1923) · Vol. 2 : Civilization and Ethics · Chapter 26 "The Civilizing Power of the Ethics of Reverence for Life"

text: Just as the wave cannot exist for itself, but is ever a part of the heaving surface of the ocean, so must I never live my life for itself, but always in the experience which is going on around me.
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: Kulturphilosophie (1923) · Vol. 2 : Civilization and Ethics · Chapter 26

text: To the question whether I am a pessimist or an optimist, I answer that my knowledge is pessimistic, but my willing and hoping are optimistic.
author: Albert Schweitzer
work: Out of My Life and Thought: An Autobiography
citation: Out of My Life and Thought : An Autobiography (1933) · Epilogue, p. 242

text: The deepest thinking is humble. It is only concerned that the flame of truth which it keeps alive should burn with the strongest and purest heat; it does not trouble about the distance to which its brightness penetrates.
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: Indian Thought And Its Development (1936) · Ch. XVI : Looking Backward and Forward, p. 257

text: The highest knowledge is to know that we are surrounded by mystery.
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: The Spiritual Life (1947) · p. 102

text: Not one of us knows what effect his life produces, and what he gives to others; that is hidden from us and must remain so, though we are often allowed to see some little fraction of it, so that we may not lose courage.
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: The Spiritual Life (1947) · p. 164

text: Profound love demands a deep conception and out of this develops reverence for the mystery of life. It brings us close to all beings, to the poorest and smallest as well as all others.
author: Albert Schweitzer
citation: Reverence for Life (1969)

text: Fear is inevitable, I have to accept that, but I cannot allow it to paralyze me.
author: Isabel Allende
citation: The Sum of Our Days: A Memoir (2007)

text: Write what should not be forgotten.
author: Isabel Allende
citation: The Japanese Lover (2015)

text: Everybody has a story and all stories are interesting if they are told in the right tone.
author: Isabel Allende
citation: from Interviews · from interviews collected on author's website

text: I think that the reason to live is to learn. We come here to experience through the body things that the spirit could not experience otherwise. So we need this body, and we have to transform this body into a temple of learning.
author: Isabel Allende
citation: from Interviews · Conversations with Isabel Allende (1999) · 1997

text: The written word is an act of human solidarity. I write so that people will love each other more.
author: Isabel Allende
citation: from Interviews · In Interviews with Latin American Writers (1989)

text: The truth is the kindest thing we can give folks in the end.
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: The Pearl of Orr's Island : A Story of the Coast of Maine (1862).

text: So much has been said and sung of beautiful young girls, why doesn’t somebody wake up to the beauty of old women?
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) · Ch 13 The Quaker Settlement

text: Any mind that is capable of a real sorrow is capable of good.
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) · Ch. 28 Reunion

text: By what strange law of mind is it that an idea long overlooked, and trodden under foot as a useless stone, suddenly sparkles out in new light, as a discovered diamond?
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) · Ch. 38.

text: To do common things perfectly is far better worth our endeavor than to do uncommon things respectably.
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: Household Papers and Stories (1864) · Ch. 10.

text: True love ennobles and dignifies the material labors of life; and homely services rendered for love’s sake have in them a poetry that is immortal.
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: Household Papers and Stories (1864) · Part 2, Ch. 4.

text: Home is a place not only of strong affections, but of entire unreserve; it is life’s undress rehearsal, its backroom, its dressing room, from which we go forth to more careful and guarded intercourse, leaving behind us much debris of cast-off and everyday clothing.
author: Harriet Beecher Stowe
citation: Little Foxes (1865) · Ch. 1.

text: I do so dearly believe that no half-heartedness and no worldly fear must turn us aside from following the light unflinchingly.
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
work: J. R. R. Tolkien: a biography
citation: 1970s · Letter to Edith, as quoted in J. R. R. Tolkien: a biography (1977) by Humphrey Carpenter, p. 66

text:
Blessed are the legend-makers with their rhyme
of things not found within recorded time.
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
citation: Mythopoeia (1931)

text: When we can take green from grass, blue from heaven, and red from blood, we have already an enchanter’s power.
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
citation: On Fairy-Stories (1939)

text: A story must be told or there’ll be no story, yet it is the untold stories that are most moving.
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
work: The Letters of J. R. R. Tolkien
citation: The Letters of J. R. R. Tolkien (1981) · No. 96: To his son Christopher (30 January 1945)

text: As children, we all live in a world of imagination, of fantasy, and for some of us that world of make-believe continues into adulthood.
author: Jim Henson
citation: It's Not Easy Being Green: And Other Things to Consider (Hyperion, 2005). · Cf. Wisdom from It's Not Easy Being Green: And Other Things to Consider (White Plains, N. Y.: Peter Pauper Press, Inc., 2007), p. 49.

text: Even as a kid, I felt isolated. Isolation makes you sensitive. As a kid, I felt I was the only person who was like that. But there’s a good side to isolation. It makes you sensitive, and sensitivity is part of the creative process.
author: Jim Henson
citation: Interview with The Boston Globe (1989)

text: There’s great value in being able to step back and laugh at yourself, at life and at attitudes. Laughter helps you put everything into perspective.
author: Jim Henson
citation: Interview with The Boston Globe (1989)

text: When you trick people into laughing at themselves, that’s wit. If you don’t laugh at yourself, everything becomes heavy.
author: Jim Henson
citation: Interview with The Boston Globe (1989)

text: The work of the eyes is done. Go now and do the heart-work on the images imprisoned within you.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Wendung (Turning Point), as translated by Stephen Mitchell

text: Make your ego porous. Will is of little importance, complaining is nothing, fame is nothing. Openness, patience, receptivity, solitude is everything.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: As quoted in Sunbeams : A Book of Quotations (1990) by Sy Safransky, p. 42

text:
They more adeptly bend the willow’s branches
who have experience of the willow’s roots.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Sonnets to Orpheus (1922) · Sonnet 6 (as translated by Edward Snow)

text: I could give you no advice but this: to go into yourself and to explore the depths where your life wells forth.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Letters to a Young Poet (1934) · Letter One (17 February 1903)

text: No experience has been too unimportant, and the smallest event unfolds like a fate, and fate itself is like a wonderful, wide fabric in which every thread is guided by an infinitely tender hand and laid alongside another thread and is held and supported by a hundred others.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Letters to a Young Poet (1934) · Letter Three (23 April 1903)

text: For one human being to love another: that is perhaps the most difficult of all our tasks, the ultimate, the last test and proof, the work for which all other work is but preparation.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Letters to a Young Poet (1934) · Letter Seven (14 May 1904)

text: If only we arrange our life according to that principle which counsels us that we must hold to the difficult, then that which now still seems to us the most alien will become what we most trust and find most faithful.
author: Rainer Maria Rilke
citation: Letters to a Young Poet (1934) · Letter Eight (12 August 1904)

text: To work — to work! It is such infinite delight to know that we still have the best things to do.
author: Katherine Mansfield
work: The Collected Letters of Katherine Mansfield
citation: Letter to Bertrand Russell (7 December 1916), from The Collected Letters of Katherine Mansfield, vol. I

text: I have made it a rule of my life never to regret and never to look back. Regret is an appalling waste of energy, and no one who intends to become a writer can afford to indulge in it. You can’t get it into shape; you can’t build on it; it’s only good for wallowing in.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: "Je ne parle pas français," from Bliss and Other Stories (1920)

text: Everything in life that we really accept undergoes a change. So suffering must become Love. This is the mystery. This is what I must do.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Journal entry (19 December 1920), published in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927) edited by J. Middleton Murry

text: The pleasure of all reading is doubled when one lives with another who shares the same books.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Letter to Ottoline Morrell (January 1922)

text: By health I mean the power to live a full, adult, living, breathing life in close contact with what I love — the earth and the wonders thereof — the sea — the sun.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Entry in her journal (10 October 1922) which she tore out to send to John Middleton Murry, before changing her mind. This later became the last published entry in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927) ed. J. Middleton Murry

text: I want, by understanding myself, to understand others. I want to be all that I am capable of becoming so that I may be (and here I have stopped and waited and waited and it’s no good — there’s only one phrase that will do) a child of the sun.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Entry in her journal (10 October 1922) which she tore out to send to John Middleton Murry, before changing her mind. This later became the last published entry in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927) ed. J. Middleton Murry

text: Warm, eager, living life — to be rooted in life — to learn, to desire to know, to feel, to think, to act. That is what I want. And nothing less.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Entry in her journal (10 October 1922) which she tore out to send to John Middleton Murry, before changing her mind. This later became the last published entry in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927) edited by J. Middleton Murry

text: I feel happy — deep down. All is well.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Entry in her journal (10 October 1922) which she tore out to send to John Middleton Murry, before changing her mind. This later became the last published entry in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927) edited by J. Middleton Murry

text: When we can begin to take our failures nonseriously, it means we are ceasing to be afraid of them. It is of immense importance to learn to laugh at ourselves.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Journal entry (October 1922), published in The Journal of Katherine Mansfield (1927)

text: Could we change our attitude, we should not only see life differently, but life itself would come to be different. Life would undergo a change of appearance because we ourselves had undergone a change of attitude.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: Quoted in A. R. Orage, "Talks with Katherine Mansfield at Fontainebleau," The Century Magazine (November 1924)

text: I always felt that the great high privilege, relief and comfort of friendship was that one had to explain nothing.
author: Katherine Mansfield
citation: As quoted in Katherine Mansfield : A Biography (1953) by Antony Alpers, p. 266

text: Love is our true destiny. We do not find the meaning of life by ourselves alone — we find it with another.
author: Thomas Merton
citation: Love and Living (1979) Part One : Love and Living, p. 27

text: The whole idea of compassion is based on a keen awareness of the interdependence of all these living beings, which are all part of one another, and all involved in one another.
author: Thomas Merton
citation: Statement from his final address, during a conference on East-West monastic dialogue, delivered just two hours before his death (10 December 1968), quoted in Religious Education, Vol. 73 (1978), p. 292, and in The Boundless Circle : Caring for Creatures and Creation (1996) by Michael W. Fox.

text: Our job is to love others without stopping to inquire whether or not they are worthy. That is not our business and, in fact, it is nobody’s business. What we are asked to do is to love, and this love itself will render both ourselves and our neighbors worthy if anything can.
author: Thomas Merton
work: Catholic Voices in a World on Fire
citation: Letter to Dorothy Day, quoted in Catholic Voices in a World on Fire (2005) by Stephen Hand, p. 180.

text: We are not meant to resolve all contradictions but to live with them and rise above them and see them in the light of exterior and objective values which make them trivial by comparison.
author: Thomas Merton
citation: Thoughts in Solitude (1956)

text: If I am a princess in rags and tatters, I can be a princess inside. It would be easy to be a princess if I were dressed in cloth of gold, but it is a great deal more of a triumph to be one all the time when no one knows it.
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
citation: A Little Princess (1905) · Chapter 11, "Ram Daas"

text: Being alive is the Magic—being strong is the Magic.
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
citation: The Secret Garden (1911) · Chapter 22

text: You know, I think everybody longs to be loved, and longs to know that he or she is lovable. And, consequently, the greatest thing that we can do is to help somebody know that they’re loved and capable of loving.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Fred Rogers: America's Favorite Neighbor (television documentary), 2003.

text: Our world hangs like a magnificent jewel in the vastness of space. Every one of us is a part of that jewel. A facet of that jewel. And in the perspective of infinity, our differences are infinitesimal.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Commencement Address at Dartmouth College June 9th, 2002

text: It’s not the honors and the prizes and the fancy outsides of life which ultimately nourish our souls. It’s the knowing that we can be trusted, that we never have to fear the truth, that the bedrock of our very being is good stuff.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Commencement Address at Middlebury College May, 2001

text: It’s our insides that make us who we are, that allow us to dream and wonder and feel for others. That’s what’s essential. That’s what will always make the biggest difference in our world.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Commencement Address at Middlebury College May, 2001

text: If only you could sense how important you are to the lives of those you meet; how important you can be to people you may never even dream of. There is something of yourself that you leave at every meeting with another person.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Mister Rogers' Neighborhood: Thoughts For All Ages

text: Children are to be respected and I respect them deeply. They’ve taught me an awful lot.
author: Fred Rogers
citation: Interviewed by Joan Rivers on The Tonight Show (1983)

text: I paint self-portraits because I am so often alone, because I am the person I know best.
author: Frida Kahlo
citation: Quotes of Frida Kahlo · 1925 - 1945 · Quoted from: Antonio Rodríguez, "Una pintora extraordinaria," Así (17 March 1945)

text: They thought I was a Surrealist, but I wasn’t. I never painted dreams. I painted my own reality.
author: Frida Kahlo
citation: Quotes of Frida Kahlo · 1946 - 1953 · Quoted in Time magazine, "Mexican Autobiography" (27 April 1953)

text: I am not sick. I am broken. But I am happy to be alive as long as I can paint.
author: Frida Kahlo
citation: Quotes of Frida Kahlo · 1946 - 1953 · Quoted in Time, "Mexican Autobiography" (27 April 1953)

text: As a writer, one has to be willing to be wrong, willing to make mistakes. I’ve put everything on the table and accepted the fact that I may come up short. And, if (or when) I do, that’s okay.
author: Nikki Giovanni
citation: “Nikki Giovanni: Interview" (2008) · NOTE: On accepting fault as a writer.

text: If I were advising someone on a writing career, the deal is this: write. If you get it published, good. If somebody pays you, better, because you have to eat, but the deal is you have to write.
author: Nikki Giovanni
citation: The Authority of a Writer (2024)

text: Let no man pull you so low as to hate him.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1950s · Sermon at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church (Montgomory, Alabama 6 Nov 1956)

text: Keep moving. Let nothing slow you up. Move on with dignity and honor and respectability.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1950s · Give Us the Ballot (1957)

text: We never get anywhere in this world without the forces of history and individual persons in the background helping us to get there.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1950s · Conquering Self-centeredness (1957)

text: Somebody must have sense enough and morality enough to cut off the chain of hate and the chain of evil in the universe. And you do that by love.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1950s · Loving Your Enemies (November 1957)

text: Hate destroys the very structure of the personality of the hater.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
