citation: 1950s · Loving Your Enemies (November 1957)

text: We must discover the power of love, the power, the redemptive power of love. And when we discover that we will be able to make of this old world a new world. We will be able to make men better. Love is the only way.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1950s · Loving Your Enemies (November 1957)

text: We must in strength and humility meet hate with love.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1950s · Loving Your Enemies (Christmas 1957)

text: The time is always right to do what’s right.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · "The Future of Integration", address in Finney Chapel at Oberlin College (22 October 1964), as quoted in "When MLK came to Oberlin" by Cindy Leise, The Chronicle-Telegram (21 January 2008); he also used a slight variant of this "the time is always right to do right" in a later speech "Remaining Awake Through a Great Revolution" delivered at Oberlin in 1965.

text: We must keep moving. If you can’t fly, run; if you can’t run, walk; if you can’t walk, crawl; but by all means keep moving.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Keep Moving from this Mountain (1960)

text: One of the sure signs of maturity is the ability to rise to the point of self criticism.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · The Rising Tide of Racial Consciousnes (1960)

text: We must combine the toughness of the serpent with the softness of the dove, a tough mind and a tender heart.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Strength to Love (1963) · Ch. 1 : A tough mind and a tender heart

text: The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy. The true neighbor will risk his position, his prestige and even his life for the welfare of others.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Strength to Love (1963) · Strength to Love, p. 25

text: Hatred paralyzes life; love releases it. Hatred confuses life; love harmonizes it. Hatred darkens life; love illuminates it.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Strength to Love (1963) · Last paragraph of section III of Antidotes for fear, page 122 (see link at top of the section)

text: There can be no deep disappointment where there is not deep love.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Letter from a Birmingham Jail (1963)

text: Dark yesterday can be transformed into bright tomorrow.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Discerning the Signs of History (1964)

text: Here and there an individual or group dares to love, and rises to the majestic heights of moral maturity. So in a real sense this is a great time to be alive.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · The Quest for Peace and Justice (1964)

text: Love is the supreme unifying principle of life.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Keep Moving From This Mountain (1965)

text: How long? Not long, because the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · How Long, Not Long (1965)

text: Oh yes, love is the way. Love is the only absolute. More and more I see this. I’ve seen too much hate to want to hate myself; hate is too great a burden to bear.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · The American Dream (1965)

text: He who lives with untruth lives in spiritual slavery. Freedom is still the bonus we receive for knowing the truth.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Why I Am Opposed to the War in Vietnam (1967) · King quoted here John F. Kennedy who at the signing of a charter establishing the German Peace Corps in Bonn, West Germany (24 June 1963) remarked: Dante once said that the hottest places in hell are reserved for those who, in a period of moral crisis, maintain their neutrality.

text: I know that love is ultimately the only answer to mankind’s problems. And I’m going to talk about it everywhere I go.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · Where Do We Go from Here: Chaos or Community? (1967)

text: You only need a heart full of grace, a soul generated by love. And you can be that servant.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · The Drum Major Instinct (1968)

text: Let us develop a kind of dangerous unselfishness.
author: Martin Luther King Jr.
citation: 1960s · I've Been to the Mountaintop (1968)

text:
Meet is it changes should control
Our being, lest we rust in ease.
We all are changed by still degrees,
All but the basis of the soul.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: "Love Thou Thy Land", st. 11 (1842)

text:
All the windy ways of men
Are but dust that rises up,
And is lightly laid again.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: "The Vision of Sin", sec. 4 (1842)

text:
Flower in the crannied wall,
I pluck you out of the crannies,
I hold you here, root and all, in my hand,
Little flower — but if I could understand
What you are, root and all, and all in all,
I should know what God and man is.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: "Flower in the Crannied Wall" (1869)

text: Love lieth deep; Love dwells not in lip-depths.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: The Lover's Tale (1879), line 466

text:
For nothing worthy proving can be proven,
Nor yet disproven: wherefore thou be wise,
Cleave ever to the sunnier side of doubt,
And cling to Faith beyond the forms of Faith!
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: From The Ancient Sage (1885), lines 66-69

text: The shell must break before the bird can fly.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: From The Ancient Sage (1885), line 154

text:
Be patient. Our Playwright may show
In some fifth act what this wild Drama means.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: The Play, reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

text:
The stream flows,
The wind blows,
The cloud fleets,
The heart beats,
Nothing will die.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: Nothing Will Die (1830)

text: There is no joy but calm!
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: The Lotos-Eaters (1832) · Choric Song, st. 2

text:
I am part of all that I have met;
Yet all experience is an arch wherethro’
Gleams that untravell’d world, whose margin fades
For ever and for ever when I move.
author: Alfred Tennyson

text:
How dull it is to pause, to make an end,
To rust unburnish’d, not to shine in use!
As tho’ to breath were life.
author: Alfred Tennyson

text: Love will conquer at the last.
author: Alfred Tennyson
citation: Locksley Hall Sixty Years After (1886) · Line 280

text: Strike up a song, my friends, and then to bed.
author: Alfred Tennyson
work: The Foresters, Robin Hood and Maid Marion
citation: The Foresters, Robin Hood and Maid Marion (1892) · Act I, Scene III

text: I still need more healthy rest in order to work at my best. My health is the main capital I have and I want to administer it intelligently.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: Letter (21 February 1952); published in Ernest Hemingway: Selected Letters 1917–1961 (1981) edited by Carlos Baker

text: We are all apprentices in a craft where no one ever becomes a master.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: New York Journal-American (11 July 1961)

text: I learned never to empty the well of my writing, but always to stop when there was still something there in the deep part of the well, and let it refill at night from the springs that fed it.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: As quoted in Reporting (1964) by Lillian Ross

text: The great thing is to last and get your work done and see and hear and learn and understand; and write when there is something that you know; and not before; and not too damned much after.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: Death in the Afternoon (1932) · Ch. 20

text: Now is no time to think of what you do not have. Think of what you can do with what there is.
author: Ernest Hemingway
work: The Old Man and the Sea
citation: The Old Man and the Sea (1952)

text: Every day is a new day. It is better to be lucky. But I would rather be exact. Then when luck comes you are ready.
author: Ernest Hemingway
work: The Old Man and the Sea
citation: The Old Man and the Sea (1952)

text: If you are lucky enough to have lived in Paris as a young man, then wherever you go for the rest of your life, it stays with you, for Paris is a moveable feast.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: A Moveable Feast (1964) · Epigraph

text: I would stand and look out over the roofs of Paris and think, “Do not worry. You have always written before and you will write now. All you have to do is write one true sentence. Write the truest sentence you know.”
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: A Moveable Feast (1964) · Ch. 2

text: You can have true affection for only a few things in your life, and by getting rid of material things, I make sure I won’t waste mine on something that can’t feel my affection.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: Papa Hemingway (1966) · Pt. 2, Ch. 5

text: The way to learn whether a person is trustworthy is to trust him.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: Papa Hemingway (1966) · Pt. 2, Ch. 6

text: Fortunately I have never learned to take the good advice I give myself nor the counsel of my fears.
author: Ernest Hemingway
citation: The Dangerous Summer (1985) · Ch. 1

text: I can’t imagine a man really enjoying a book and reading it only once.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Letter to Arthur Greeves (February 1932); in They Stand Together: The Letters of C. S. Lewis to Arthur Greeves, 1914–1963 (1979), p. 439

text: I think that if God forgives us we must forgive ourselves. Otherwise it is almost like setting up ourselves as a higher tribunal than Him.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Letter (19 April 1951); in Letters of C. S. Lewis (1966), p. 230

text: Where we find a difficulty we may always expect that a discovery awaits us. Where there is cover we hope for game.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Reflections on the Psalms (1958), ch. III: Cursings

text: The very man who has argued you down will sometimes be found, years later, to have been influenced by what you said.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Reflections on the Psalms (1958), ch. VII: Connivance, p. 73

text: There are some things about your own village that you never know until you have been away from it.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Studies in Words (1960), ch. 11

text: A pleasure is full grown only when it is remembered.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Out of the Silent Planet (1938) · Hyoi, p. 73

text: Gratitude looks to the past and love to the present; fear, avarice, lust, and ambition look ahead.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The Screwtape Letters (1942) · Letter XVI

text: My form remains one, though the matter in it changes continually. I am, in that respect, like a curve in a waterfall.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Miracles (1947) · Ch. 16: "Miracles of the New Creation"

text: Perfect humility dispenses with modesty.
author: C. S. Lewis
work: The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses
citation: The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses (1949) · "The Weight of Glory"

text: We live, in fact, in a world starved for solitude, silence, and privacy: and therefore starved for meditation and true friendship.
author: C. S. Lewis
work: The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses
citation: The Weight of Glory and Other Addresses (1949) · "Membership"

text: Some day you will be old enough to start reading fairy tales again.
author: C. S. Lewis
work: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
citation: The Chronicles of Narnia (1950–1956) · The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (1950), Dedication: "To Lucy Barfield"

text: A proud man is always looking down on things and people: and, of course, as long as you are looking down, you cannot see something that is above you.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Mere Christianity (1952) · Book III, Chapter 8, "The Great Sin"

text: If I find in myself a desire which no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Mere Christianity (1952) · Book III, Chapter 10, "Hope"

text: But how can the characters in a play guess the plot? We are not the playwright, we are not the producer, we are not even the audience. We are on the stage. To play well the scenes in which we are “on” concerns us much more than to guess about the scenes that follow it.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The World's Last Night (1952)

text: Eating and reading are two pleasures that combine admirably.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Surprised by Joy (1955) · Ch. IX: "The Great Knock"

text: Enough had been thought, and said, and felt, and imagined. It was about time that something should be done.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Surprised by Joy (1955) · Ch. XIV

text: Nothing is yet in its true form.
author: C. S. Lewis
work: Till We Have Faces: A Myth Retold
citation: Till We Have Faces: A Myth Retold (1956) · Pt. 2, IV

text: We are born helpless. As soon as we are fully conscious we discover loneliness. We need others physically, emotionally, intellectually; we need them if we are to know anything, even ourselves.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The Four Loves (1960) · Introduction

text: Friendship is unnecessary, like philosophy, like art, like the universe itself (for God did not need to create). It has no survival value; rather it is one of those things which give value to survival.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The Four Loves (1960) · Ch. IV

text: To love at all is to be vulnerable.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: The Four Loves (1960) · Ch. VI: "Charity"

text: It’s so much easier to pray for a bore than to go and see one.
author: C. S. Lewis
work: Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer
citation: Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer (1963)

text: The Value of myth is that it takes all the things you know and restores to them the rich significance which has been hidden by the veil of familiarity.
author: C. S. Lewis
citation: Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings · p. 90

text: It is the hardest thing in the world to frighten a mongoose, because he is eaten up from nose to tail with curiosity. The motto of all the mongoose family is “Run and find out,” and Rikki-tikki was a true mongoose.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: The Jungle Book (1894) · Rikki-Tikki-Tavi

text: For the strength of the Pack is the Wolf, and the strength of the Wolf is the Pack.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: The Second Jungle Book (1895) · The Law of the Jungle, Stanzas 1 and 2.

text:
If you can fill the unforgiving minute
With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run,
Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it,
And—which is more—you’ll be a Man, my son!
author: Rudyard Kipling

text:
I keep six honest serving-men:
(They taught me all I knew)
Their names are What and Where and When
And How and Why and Who.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Just So Stories (1902) · The Elephant's Child.

text: Enough work to do, and strength enough to do the work.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · A Doctor's Work, an address at Middlesex Hospital (October 1908).

text: Words are, of course, the most powerful drug used by mankind.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · Speech, quoted in The Times (February 15, 1923).

text: More men are killed by overwork than the importance of the world justifies.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · The Phantom 'Rickshaw (1888).

text:
Ever the wide world over, lass,
Ever the trail held true,
Over the world and under the world,
And back at the last to you.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · The Gypsy Trail, Stanza 2 (1892).

text:
God gave all men all earth to love,
But since our hearts are small,
Ordained for each one spot should prove
Belovèd over all.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · Sussex, Stanza 1 (1902).

text:
Something hidden. Go and find it. Go and look behind the Ranges—
Something lost behind the Ranges. Lost and waiting for you. Go!
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · The Explorer, Stanza 2 (1903).

text: Fiction is Truth’s elder sister. Obviously. No one in the world knew what truth was till some one had told a story.
author: Rudyard Kipling
citation: Other works · "Fiction", speech to the Royal Society of Literature, June 1926; published in Writings on Writing: Rudyard Kipling (1996), ed. Sandra Kemp and Lisa Lewis, p. 80

text: Progress consists, not in the increase of truth, but in freeing it from its wrappings. The truth is obtained like gold, not by letting it grow bigger, but by washing off from it everything that isn’t gold.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: Tolstoy's Diaries (1985) edited and translated by R. F. Christian. London: Athlone Press, Vol 2, p. 512

text: There is only one enduring happiness in life—to live for others.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: Family Happiness (1859) · Part 1, chapter 2

text: Seize the moments of happiness, love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world, all else is folly. It is the one thing we are interested in here.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Book IV, Ch. 11

text: The only thing that we know is that we know nothing — and that is the highest flight of human wisdom.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Book V, Ch. I

text: The strongest of all warriors are these two — Time and Patience.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Bk. X, ch. 16

text: To love life is to love God. Harder and more blessed than all else is to love this life in one’s sufferings, in undeserved sufferings.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Bk. XIV, ch. 15

text: Pure and complete sorrow is as impossible as pure and complete joy.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: War and Peace (1865–1867; 1869) · Bk. XV, ch. 1

text: I have learnt that all men live not by care for themselves, but by love.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: What Men Live By (1881) · Ch. XII

text: To be good and lead a good life means to give to others more than one takes from them.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: The First Step (1892) · Ch. VII

text: By words one transmits thoughts to another, by means of art, one transmits feelings.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: What is Art? (1897)

text: Humanity unceasingly strives forward from a lower, more partial and obscure understanding of life to one more general and more lucid.
author: Leo Tolstoy
citation: What is Art? (1897)

text: To be angry with a man is to hate him; to hate him is to wish him harm; but to wish him well, even if he has done you harm, is the mark of a great mind.
author: Seneca
citation: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira) 2.34.5 (translated by John W. Basore)

text: Lay hold of today’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon tomorrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter I: On Saving Time

text: The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter II: On discursiveness in reading

text: “What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.” That was indeed a great benefit; such a person can never be alone. You may be sure that such a man is a friend to all mankind.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter VI: On precepts and exemplars · Seneca is quoting Hecato.

text: If you would not have a man flinch when the crisis comes, train him before it comes.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XVIII: On Festivals and Fasting

text: It is indeed foolish to be unhappy now because you may be unhappy at some future time.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XXIV: On despising death

text: I do not know whether I shall make progress; but I should prefer to lack success rather than to lack faith.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XXV: On Reformation

text: You need a change of soul rather than a change of climate.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

text: You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

text: “You will have less money.” Yes, and less trouble. “Less influence.” Yes, and less envy.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XLII: On Values

text: He that owns himself has lost nothing. But how few men are blessed with ownership of self!
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XLII: On Values

text: That which Fortune has not given, she cannot take away.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter LIX: On Pleasure and Joy

text: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter LXI: On meeting death cheerfully

text: Let us greedily enjoy our friends, because we do not know how long this privilege will be ours.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter LXIII

text: No man can suffer both severely and for a long time; Nature, who loves us most tenderly, has so constituted us as to make pain either endurable or short.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

text: Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

text: As our acts and our thoughts are, so will our lives be.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XCV: On the usefulness of basic principles

text: Accept in an unruffled spirit that which is inevitable.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter XCIX: On Consolation to the Bereaved

text: Therefore, my dear Lucilius, begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.
author: Seneca
citation: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) · Letter CI: On the Futility of Planning Ahead

text: Apply reason to difficulties; harsh circumstances can be softened, narrow limits can be widened, and burdensome things can be made to press less severely on those who bear them cleverly.
author: Seneca
citation: On Tranquility of the Mind

text: Mankind is born for mutual assistance, anger for mutual ruin: the former loves society, the latter estrangement.
author: Seneca
citation: Dialogues · On Anger to Novatus

text: The mind must be indulged, and leisure must be given from time to time, which is the place of food and strength.
author: Seneca
citation: Dialogues · Dialogi de Tranquillitate Animi (Concerning Peace of Mind)

text: Right is of no sex, Truth is of no color, God is the Father of us all, and we are all Brethren.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: Douglass' chosen motto for his weekly publication The North Star. It appeared on the first issue. As quoted in Maurice S. Lee (2009), The Cambridge Companion to Frederick Douglass. Cambridge University Press, p. 50; Thomson, Conyers & Dawson (2009). The Frederick Douglass Encyclopedia. ABC-CLIO. p. 149; & Connie A. Miller. Frederick Douglass American Hero: And International Icon of the Nineteenth Century. Xlibris Corporation. p. 144

text: I prefer to be true to myself, even at the hazard of incurring the ridicule of others, rather than to be false, and incur my own abhorrence.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1840s · Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, An American Slave (1845) · Ch. 5

text: Though conscious of the difficulty of learning without a teacher, I set out with high hope, and a fixed purpose, at whatever cost of trouble, to learn how to read.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1840s · Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, An American Slave (1845) · Ch. 6

text: I would unite with anybody to do right; and with nobody to do wrong.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1850s · Lecture, The Anti-Slavery Movement (1855)

text: Men might not get all they work for in this world, but they must certainly work for all they get.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1850s · West India Emancipation (1857)

text: I do not ask you about the dead past. I bring you to the living present.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1860s · Should the Negro Enlist in the Union Army? (1863)

text: Personal independence is a virtue and it is the soul out of which comes the sturdiest manhood. But there can be no independence without a large share of self-dependence, and this virtue cannot be bestowed. It must be developed from within.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1870s · Self-Made Men (1872)

text: I believe in individuality, but individuals are, to the mass, like waves to the ocean. The highest order of genius is as dependent as is the lowest.
author: Frederick Douglass
citation: 1870s · Self-Made Men (1872)

text: Just as the constant increase of entropy is the basic law of the universe, so it is the basic law of life to be ever more highly structured and to struggle against entropy.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Letter to Husák

text: The salvation of this human world lies nowhere else than in the human heart, in the human power to reflect, in human meekness and human responsibility.
author: Václav Havel
citation: International Herald Tribune (21 February 1990)

text: The only lost cause is one we give up on before we enter the struggle.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Quoted in Amnesty International's essay "From Prisoner to President – A Tribute"

text: Anyone who takes himself too seriously always runs the risk of looking ridiculous; anyone who can consistently laugh at himself does not.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Disturbing the Peace (1986) · Ch. 2 : Writing for the Stage

text: The real test of a man is not how well he plays the role he has invented for himself, but how well he plays the role that destiny assigned to him.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Disturbing the Peace (1986) · Ch. 2 : Writing for the Stage, p. 72

text: Hope is definitely not the same thing as optimism. It is not the conviction that something will turn out well, but the certainty that something makes sense, regardless of how it turns out.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Disturbing the Peace (1986) · Ch. 5 : The Politics of Hope

text: Sober perseverance is more effective than enthusiastic emotions, which are all too capable of being transferred, with little difficulty, to something different each day.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Disturbing the Peace (1986) · Ch. 5 : The Politics of Hope, p. 111

text: The deeper the experience of an absence of meaning — in other words, of absurdity — the more energetically meaning is sought.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Disturbing the Peace (1986) · Ch. 5

text: There are times when we must sink to the bottom of our misery to understand truth, just as we must descend to the bottom of a well to see the stars in broad daylight.
author: Václav Havel
citation: Living in Truth (1986) · The Power of the Powerless

text: Self-confidence is not pride. Just the contrary: only a person or a nation that is self-confident, in the best sense of the word, is capable of listening to others, accepting them as equals, forgiving its enemies and regretting its own guilt.
author: Václav Havel
citation: New Year's Address to the Nation (1990)

text: What I do is me: for that I came.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: "As Kingfishers Catch Fire, Dragonflies Draw Flame" (undated poem, c. March - April 1877) - Analysis and information regarding this poem at the Gerard Manley Hopkins Society

text:
Elected Silence, sing to me
And beat upon my whorlèd ear,
Pipe me to pastures still and be
The music that I care to hear.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The Habit of Perfection", lines 1-4

text:
The world is charged with the grandeur of God.
It will flame out, like shining from shook foil;
It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil
Crushed.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "God's Grandeur", lines 1-4

text: There lives the dearest freshness deep down things.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "God's Grandeur," line 10

text:
Look at the stars! look, look up at the skies!
O look at all the fire-folk sitting in the air!
The bright boroughs, the circle-citadels there!
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The Starlight Night" (1877), lines 1-3

author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "Pied Beauty", lines 1-3

text:
Ask of her, the mighty mother:
Her reply puts this other
Question: What is Spring?—
Growth in everything.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The May Magnificat", stanza 4

text:
What would the world be, once bereft
Of wet and of wildness? Let them be left,
O let them be left, wildness and wet;
Long live the weeds and the wilderness yet.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "Inversnaid, lines 13-16

text:
I say that we are wound
With mercy round and round
As if with air.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "The Blessed Virgin compared to the Air we Breathe", lines 34-36

text:
My own heart let me have more have pity on; let
Me live to my sad self hereafter kind,
Charitable; not live this tormented mind
With this tormented mind tormenting yet.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "My own heart let me have more have pity on", lines 1-4

text: Mine, O thou lord of life, send my roots rain.
author: Gerard Manley Hopkins
citation: Wessex Poems and Other Verses (1918) · "Thou art indeed just, Lord, if I contend", line 14

text: One can never consent to creep when one feels an impulse to soar.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Address to the American Association to Promote the Teaching of Speech to the Deaf at Mt. Airy, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (8 July 1896), quoted in supplement to The Story of My Life

text: We differ, blind and seeing, one from another, not in our senses, but in the use we make of them, in the imagination and courage with which we seek wisdom beyond the senses.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Five-sensed World (1910)

text: When one door of happiness closes, another opens; but often we look so long at the closed door that we do not see the one which has been opened for us.
author: Helen Keller
citation: We Bereaved (1929)

text: Believe, when you are most unhappy, that there is something for you to do in the world. So long as you can sweeten another’s pain, life is not in vain.
author: Helen Keller
citation: We Bereaved (1929)

text: Many persons have a wrong of idea of what constitutes true happiness. It is not attained through self-gratification but through fidelity to a worthy purpose.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Helen Keller's Journal: 1936-1937 (1938), p. 57

text: Security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature, nor do the children of men as a whole experience it. Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Open Door (1957) This quotation is often contracted into: Security is mostly a superstition... Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing. or paraphrased: Life is either a daring adventure or nothing at all.

text: I do not want the peace that passeth understanding. I want the understanding which bringeth peace.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Quoted in Henry More: The Rational Theology of a Cambridge Plattonist (1962) by Rabbi Aharon Lichtenstein, page 100

text: I would rather walk with a friend in the dark than walk alone in the light.
author: Helen Keller
citation: "Helen and Teacher: The Story of Helen Keller and Anne Sullivan Macy", Joseph P. Lash (1980)

text: It seemed to me that there could be nothing more beautiful than the sun, whose warmth makes all things grow.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Story of My Life (1903) · Ch. 6

text: The beautiful truth burst upon my mind — I felt that there were invisible lines stretched between my spirit and the spirits of others.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Story of My Life (1903) · Ch. 6

text: I have found out that though the ways in which I can make myself useful are few, yet the work open to me is endless.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Optimism (1903)

text: I trust, and nothing that happens disturbs my trust.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Optimism (1903)

text: Optimism, then, is a fact within my own heart. But as I look out upon life, my heart meets no contradiction. The outward world justifies my inward universe of good.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Optimism (1903)

text: Optimism is the faith that leads to achievement; nothing can be done without hope.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Optimism (1903)

text: So long as the memory of certain beloved friends lives in my heart I shall say that life is good.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Midstream (1929)

text: I who cannot see find hundreds of things to interest me through mere touch.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Three Days to See (1933)

text: I feel the delightful, velvety texture of a flower, and discover its remarkable convolutions; and something of the miracle of Nature is revealed to me.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Three Days to See (1933)

text: Use your eyes as if tomorrow you would be stricken blind.
author: Helen Keller
citation: Three Days to See (1933)

text: A happy life consists not in the absence, but in the mastery of hardships.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Simplest Way to be Happy (1933)

text: It all comes to this: the simplest way to be happy is to do good.
author: Helen Keller
citation: The Simplest Way to be Happy (1933)

text: Where is human nature so weak as in a book store?
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: "Subtleties of Book Buyers," Star Papers (1855)

text: A library is not a luxury, but one of the necessaries of life.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: Eyes and Ears (1862)

text: The call to religion is not a call to be better than your fellows, but to be better than yourself.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: Life Thoughts (1858) · p. 22

text: Greatness lies not in being strong, but in the right using of strength; and strength is not used rightly when it only serves to carry a man above his fellows for his own solitary glory. He is greatest whose strength carries up the most hearts by the attraction of his own.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: Life Thoughts (1858) · p. 52

text: There is no such thing as preaching patience into people, unless the sermon is so long that they have to practise it while they hear.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: Life Thoughts (1858) · p. 61

text: The first hour of the morning is the rudder of the day.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: Life Thoughts (1858) · p. 95

text: Flowers are the sweetest things that God ever made, and forgot to put a soul into.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: Life Thoughts (1858) · p. 234

text: The truth is larger than any one man’s thought of it. The truth of God usually has relations that stretch out in such a way that men may see it very differently, and all of them be true in spots, although they do not have the whole truth.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: The Nature, Importance and Liberties of Belief (1873)

text: Everyman is full of music, but it is not everyman that knows how to bring it out.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
citation: Proverbs from Plymouth Pulpit (1887)

text: Difficulties are God’s errands; and when we are sent upon them, we should esteem it a proof of God’s confidence, — as a compliment from God.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895) · p. 107

text: Success is full of promise till men get it; and then it is last year’s nest from which the bird has flown.
author: Henry Ward Beecher
work: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers
citation: Dictionary of Burning Words of Brilliant Writers (1895) · p. 567

text:
If thou must love me, let it be for nought
Except for love’s sake only.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
citation: Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850) · No. XIV

text: How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
citation: Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850) · No. XLIII

text:
Every wish
Is like a prayer—with God.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
citation: Aurora Leigh (1857) · Bk. II

text:
Whoso loves
Believes the impossible.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
citation: Aurora Leigh (1857) · Bk. V

text:
Whatever’s lost, it first was won;
We will not struggle nor impugn.
Perhaps the cup was broken here,
That Heaven’s new wine might show more clear.
I praise Thee while my days go on.
author: Elizabeth Barrett Browning
citation: Last Poems (1862) · "De Profundis", st. 22

text: Children are a wonderful gift. They have an extraordinary capacity to see into the heart of things and to expose sham and humbug for what they are.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: As quoted in "The Words of Desmond Tutu" (1984)

text: A person is a person because he recognizes others as persons.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: Address at his enthronement as Anglican archbishop of Cape Town (7 September 1986)

text: You don’t choose your family. They are God’s gift to you, as you are to them.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: Address at his enthronement as Anglican archbishop of Cape Town (7 September 1986)

text: Resentment and anger are bad for your blood pressure and your digestion.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: As quoted in "Truth and reconciliation" at BBC Focus on Africa (January-March 2000)

text: Without forgiveness there can be no future for a relationship between individuals or within and between nations.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: As quoted in "Truth and reconciliation" at BBC Focus on Africa (January-March 2000)

text: We may be surprised at the people we find in heaven. God has a soft spot for sinners. His standards are quite low.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: As quoted in The Mammoth Book of Zingers, Quips, and One-Liners (2004) by Geoff Tibballs, p. 255

text: All are to be held in the incredible embrace of the love that won’t let us go.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: "And God Smiles," sermon preached at All Saints Church, Pasadena, California (6 November 2005)

text: Sometimes you want to whisper in God’s ear, “God, we know you are in charge, but why don’t you make it slightly more obvious?”
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: Wallenberg Lecture (2008)

text: You and I are created for transcendence, laughter, caring. God deliberately did not make the world perfect, for God is looking for you and me to be fellow workers with God.
author: Desmond Tutu
citation: Wallenberg Lecture (2008)

text: Fortunate is he who does not carry envy as a companion.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · I, 431 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text: If you wish mercy, show mercy to the weak.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · I, 822 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text: Many of the faults you see in others, dear reader, are your own nature reflected in them.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · I, 1319 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text: The lion who breaks the enemy’s ranks is a minor hero compared to the lion who overcomes himself.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · I, 1389

text: If you are wholly perplexed and in straits, have patience, for patience is the key to joy.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · I, 2908 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text: If you are irritated by every rub, how will your mirror be polished?
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · I, 2980 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text: God turns you from one feeling to another and teaches by means of opposites, so that you will have two wings to fly, not one.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · II, 1552; 1554 (tr. Helminski, 1990)

text:
If an ant seeks the rank of Solomon,
don’t smile contemptuously upon its quest.
Everything you possess of skill, and wealth and handicraft,
wasn’t it first merely a thought and a quest?
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · III, 1445-49 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

text:
Come, seek, for search is the foundation of fortune:
Every success depends upon focusing the heart.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · III, 2302-5 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

text:
That which God said to the rose,
and caused it to laugh in full-blown beauty,
He said to my heart,
and made it a hundred times more beautiful.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · III, 4129 (tr. Helminski, 1996)

text:
Everyone sees the unseen in proportion to the clarity of his heart, and that depends upon how much he has polished it.
Whoever has polished it more sees more — more unseen forms become manifest to him.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · IV, 2909-10 (tr. Chittick)

text:
The branch might seem like the fruit’s origin:
In fact, the branch exists because of the fruit.
author: Rumi
citation: Masnavi · "You Are the Macrocosm" (tr. Andrew Harvey, 1999)

author: Rumi
citation: Divan-i Shams · 1740:1-3 (tr. Fatemeh Keshavarz, 1998)

text: It is a beautiful truth that all men contain something of the artist in them. And perhaps it is the case that the greatest artists live and die, the world and themselves alike ignorant what they possess.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: "Talk to an Art-Union (A Brooklyn fragment)" (1839); later delivered as a lecture at the Brooklyn Art Union (31 March 1851) and printed in the Brooklyn Daily Advertizer (3 April 1851)

text: None has begun to think how divine he himself is and how certain the future is.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Starting from Paumanok. 7

text: I loafe and invite my soul.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Song of Myself, 1

text: I have no mockings or arguments; I witness and wait.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Song of Myself, 4

text: In the faces of men and women I see God.
author: Walt Whitman
citation: Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Song of Myself, 48

text:
Each of us inevitable;
Each of us limitless—each of us with his or her right upon the earth.
