And then there crept
A little noiseless noise among the leaves,
Born of the very sigh that silence heaves.
author: John Keats
citation: Poems (1817) · "I Stood Tiptoe", l. 10

text:
To one who has been long in city pent,
’Tis very sweet to look into the fair
And open face of heaven.
author: John Keats
citation: Poems (1817) · "Sonnet. To One Who Has Been Long in City Pent"

text: The poetry of earth is never dead.
author: John Keats
citation: Poems (1817) · "Sonnet. On the Grasshopper and the Cricket"

text:
A thing of beauty is a joy forever:
Its loveliness increases; it will never
Pass into nothingness; but still will keep
A bower quiet for us, and a sleep
Full of sweet dreams, and health, and quiet breathing.
author: John Keats
citation: Endymion (1818) · Bk. I, l. 1

text:
In spite of all,
Some shape of beauty moves away the pall
From our dark spirits.
author: John Keats
citation: Endymion (1818) · Bk. I, l. 11

text:
O magic sleep! O comfortable bird,
That broodest o’er the troubled sea of the mind
Till it is hush’d and smooth!
author: John Keats
citation: Endymion (1818) · Bk. I, l. 453

text:
Time, that aged nurse,
Rocked me to patience.
author: John Keats
citation: Endymion (1818) · Bk. I, l. 705

text:
Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard
Are sweeter: therefore, ye soft pipes, play on;
Not to the sensual ear, but, more endear’d,
Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone.
author: John Keats
citation: Poems (1820) · Ode on a Grecian Urn · Stanza 2

text:
“Beauty is truth, truth beauty,” — that is all
Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know.
author: John Keats
citation: Poems (1820) · Ode on a Grecian Urn · Stanza 5. The final lines of this poem have been rendered in various ways in different editions, some placing the entire last two lines within quotation marks, others only the statement "Beauty is truth, truth beauty," and others without any quotation marks. The poet's final intentions upon the matter before his death are unclear.

text: I live from day to day, and content myself with having enough to meet my present and ordinary needs; for the extraordinary, all the provision in the world could not suffice.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book I · Ch. 14

text: Things are not so painful and difficult of themselves, but our weakness or cowardice makes them so.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book I · Ch. 14 (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: We must not attach knowledge to the mind, we have to incorporate it there.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book I · Ch. 25

text: There are some defeats more triumphant than victories.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book I · Ch. 30. Of Cannibals (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Hazlitt, 1842)

text: There is as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and others.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book II · Ch. 1. Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions (tr. Cotton, rev. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)

text: There were never in the world two opinions alike, any more than two hairs or two grains. Their most universal quality is diversity.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book II · Ch. 37

text: Lend yourself to others, but give yourself to yourself.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book III · Ch. 10. Of Managing the Will

text: There is no wish more natural than the wish to know.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book III · Ch. 13

text: Let us give Nature a chance; she knows her business better than we do.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Book III · Ch. 13

text: There is, nevertheless, a certain respect and a general duty of humanity that ties us, not only to beasts that have life and sense, but even to trees and plants.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Book II, Ch. 11. Of Cruelty

text: When I play with my cat, who knows whether I do not make her more sport than she makes me?
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Book II, Ch. 12. Apology for Raimond Sebond

text: Arts and sciences are not cast in a mould, but are formed and perfected by degrees, by often handling and polishing, as bears leisurely lick their cubs into form.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Book II, Ch. 12. Apology for Raimond Sebond

text: The mariner of old said to Neptune in a great tempest, “O God! thou mayest save me if thou wilt, and if thou wilt thou mayest destroy me; but whether or no, I will steer my rudder true.”
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Book II, Ch. 16. Of Glory

text: Nature forms us for ourselves, not for others; to be, not to seem.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Book II, Ch. 37. Of the Resemblance of Children to their Brothers

text: I have here only made a nosegay of culled flowers, and have brought nothing of my own but the thread that ties them together.
author: Michel de Montaigne
citation: Essais (wr. 1571–92; pub. 1580–95) · Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919) · Book III, Ch. 12. Of Physiognomy

text: I was given the freedom to discover my own inclination and talents, to fashion my inmost pleasures and sorrows myself and to regard the future not as an alien higher power but as the hope and product of my own strength.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Gertrude (1910) · p. 4

text: That is where my dearest and brightest dreams have ranged — to hear for the duration of a heartbeat the universe and the totality of life in its mysterious, innate harmony.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Gertrude (1910)

text: Man’s life seems to me like a long, weary night that would be intolerable if there were not occasionally flashes of light, the sudden brightness of which is so comforting and wonderful, that the moments of their appearance cancel out and justify the years of darkness.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Gertrude (1910)

text: We cannot evade life’s course, but we can school ourselves to be superior to fortune and also to look unflinchingly upon the most painful things.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Gertrude (1910) · p. 236

text: No man has ever been entirely and completely himself. Yet each one strives to become that — one in an awkward, the other in a more intelligent way, each as best he can.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Demian (1919) · p. 9 Prologue

text: You must find your dream, then the way becomes easy. But there is no dream that lasts forever, each dream is followed by another, and one should not cling to any particular one.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Demian (1919) · p. 94

text: The tree does not die. It waits.
author: Hermann Hesse

text: Whether you and I and a few others will renew the world someday remains to be seen. But within ourselves we must renew it each day, otherwise we just aren’t serious. Don’t forget that!
author: Hermann Hesse

text: Everyone can perform magic, everyone can reach his goals, if he is able to think, if he is able to wait, if he is able to fast.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Siddhartha (1922) · As translated by Ejvind Haas

text: What could I say to you that would be of value, except that perhaps you seek too much, that as a result of your seeking you cannot find.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Siddhartha (1922) · H. Rosner, trans. (Bantam: 1971), p. 140

text: Never is a man or a deed wholly Samsara or wholly Nirvana; never is a man wholly a saint or a sinner.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Siddhartha (1922)

text: Words do not express thoughts very well. They always become a little different immediately after they are expressed, a little distorted, a little foolish. And yet it also pleases me and seems right that what is of value and wisdom to one man seems nonsense to another.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Siddhartha (1922)

text: There was room for repentance and solitude; room for good living and company.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: Narcissus and Goldmund (1930)

text:
Since life may summon us at every age
Be ready, heart, for parting, new endeavor,
Be ready bravely and without remorse
To find new light that old ties cannot give.
author: Hermann Hesse
citation: The Glass Bead Game (1943) · Stages

text: Genius will live and thrive without training, but it does not the less reward the watering-pot and pruning-knife.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: "Life of Sir James Mackintosh" in Papers on Literature and Art (1846), p. 50

text: Very early, I knew that the only object in life was to grow.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Memoirs of Margaret Fuller Ossoli (1852), Vol. I, p. 132

text: To one who has enjoyed the full life of any scene, of any hour, what thoughts can be recorded about it, seem like the commas and semicolons in the paragraph, mere stops.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Summer on the Lakes, in 1843 (1844) · p. 10

text: All around us lies what we neither understand nor use. Our capacities, our instincts for this our present sphere are but half developed.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Summer on the Lakes, in 1843 (1844) · "Good Sense" in a dialogue between Free Hope, Old Church, Good Sense, and Self -Poise. p. 127

text: Only the dreamer shall understand realities, though, in truth, his dreaming must not be out of proportion to his waking!
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Summer on the Lakes, in 1843 (1844) · "Free Hope" p. 127

text: To me it seems that it is madder never to abandon oneself, than often to be infatuated; better to be wounded, a captive, and a slave, than always to walk in armor.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Summer on the Lakes, in 1843 (1844) · "Free Hope" p. 131

text: Let us be wise, and not impede the soul.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845)

text: Plants of great vigor will almost always struggle into blossom, despite impediments. But there should be encouragement, and a free genial atmosphere for those of more timid sort, fair play for each in its own kind.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845)

text: Always the soul says to us all, Cherish your best hopes as a faith, and abide by them in action. Such shall be the effectual fervent means to their fulfilment.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845)

text:
With equal sweetness the commissioned hours
Shed light and dew upon both weeds and flowers.
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Life Without and Life Within (1859) · The Thankful and the Thankless

text:
Live earnestly by turns without despair,
Nor seek a home till home be every where!
author: Margaret Fuller
citation: Life Without and Life Within (1859) · The One In All

text: Writing to me is an advanced and slow form of reading. If you find a book you really want to read but it hasn’t been written yet, then you must write it.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: Morrison said this in her talk at the annual meeting of the Ohio Arts Council in Cincinnati in September 1981. Variants, unsourced:

text: All water has a perfect memory and is forever trying to get back to where it was.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: As quoted in Grace Notes (1989) by Rita Dove

text: I remember a very important lesson that my father gave me when I was twelve or thirteen. He said, “You know, today I welded a perfect seam and I signed my name to it.” And I said, “But, Daddy, no one’s going to see it!” And he said, “Yeah, but I know it’s there.”
author: Toni Morrison
citation: As quoted in the New York Times Magazine (11 September 1994).

text: You free. Nothing and nobody is obliged to save you but you.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: Home (novella), p. 126 (2012)

text: If you surrendered to the air, you could ride it.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: Song of Solomon (1977)

text: Human life is holy, all of it.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: Beloved (1987)

text: The vitality of language lies in its ability to limn the actual, imagined and possible lives of its speakers, readers, writers.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: Nobel Prize Lecture (1993)

text: Language alone protects us from the scariness of things with no names. Language alone is meditation.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: Nobel Prize Lecture (1993)

text: For me, Art is the restoration of order. It may discuss all sort of terrible things, but there must be satisfaction at the end. A little bit of hunger, but also satisfaction.
author: Toni Morrison
citation: from interviews and conversations · Interview with Don Swaim (1987)

text: Not everything that is faced can be changed; but nothing can be changed until it is faced.
author: James Baldwin
work: The New York Times Book Review
citation: "As Much Truth As One Can Bear" in The New York Times Book Review (January 14, 1962); republished in The Cross of Redemption: Uncollected Writings (2011), edited by Randall Kenan

text: Despair is a sin. I believe that. It is easy to be bleak about the human race, but there are people who have proved to me that we can be better than we are.
author: James Baldwin
citation: Interview with M. S. Handler of the New York Times (3 June 1964), quoted in 'Demand For Presidential Lead On U.S. Race Issue', The Times (4 June 1963), p. 10

text: One must say Yes to life, and embrace it wherever it is found — and it is found in terrible places.
author: James Baldwin
citation: From Nothing Personal, a collaboration with the photographer Richard Avedon (1964). Baldwin's text for the volume can be found "here".

text: You’ve got to tell the world how to treat you. If the world tells you how you are going to be treated, you are in trouble.
author: James Baldwin
citation: James Baldwin and Margaret Mead: A Rap on Race, p. 95. J. B. Lippincott, 1971.

text: For, while the tale of how we suffer, and how we are delighted, and how we may triumph is never new, it always must be heard. There isn’t any other tale to tell, it’s the only light we’ve got in all this darkness.
author: James Baldwin
citation: Sonny's Blues (1957)

text: Art would not be important if life were not important, and life is important.
author: James Baldwin
citation: "An interview with James Baldwin" (1961)

text: I think that mankind can do better than that, and I wish to be a witness to this small and stubborn possibility.
author: James Baldwin
citation: "The War Crimes Tribunal" (1967)

text: There is a reason, after all, that some people wish to colonize the moon, and others dance before it as before an ancient friend.
author: James Baldwin
citation: No Name in the Street (1972)

text: Close up, the person’s imperfections matter, but from far away, you see your own.
author: James Baldwin
citation: Just Above My Head (1979)

text: It is not merely that the rain falls differently on each of you, for that can be a wonder and a joy: it is that what is rain for the one is not rain for the other.
author: James Baldwin
citation: Just Above My Head (1979)

text: Perhaps the turning point in one’s life is realizing that to be treated like a victim is not necessarily to become one.
author: James Baldwin
citation: Conversations with James Baldwin (1961 to 1988) · 1984

text: It does not matter much whom we live with in this world, but it matters a great deal whom we dream of.
author: Willa Cather
citation: Youth and the Bright Medusa, "A Gold Slipper" (1920)

text: Only solitary men know the full joys of friendship. Others have their family — but to a solitary and an exile his friends are everything.
author: Willa Cather
citation: Shadows on the Rock (1931), Book III, Ch. 5

text: Sometimes a neighbor whom we have disliked a lifetime for his arrogance and conceit lets fall a single commonplace remark that shows us another side, another man, really; a man uncertain, and puzzled, and in the dark like ourselves.
author: Willa Cather
citation: Shadows on the Rock (1931), Epilogue

text: There are only two or three human stories, and they go on repeating themselves as fiercely as if they had never happened before; like the larks in this country, that have been singing the same five notes over for thousands of years.
author: Willa Cather
citation: O Pioneers! (1913) · Part II, Ch. 4

text: I like trees because they seem more resigned to the way they have to live than other things do.
author: Willa Cather
citation: O Pioneers! (1913) · Part II, Ch. 8

text: We come and go, but the land is always here. And the people who love it and understand it are the people who own it — for a little while.
author: Willa Cather
citation: O Pioneers! (1913) · Part V, Ch. 3

text: Every artist makes himself born. It is very much harder than the other time, and longer.
author: Willa Cather
citation: The Song of the Lark (1915) · Part II, Ch. 3

text: What was any art but an effort to make a sheath, a mould in which to imprison for a moment the shining, elusive element which is life itself — life hurrying past us and running away, too strong to stop, too sweet to lose?
author: Willa Cather
citation: The Song of the Lark (1915) · Part IV, Ch. 3

text: There are some things you learn best in calm, and some in storm.
author: Willa Cather
citation: The Song of the Lark (1915) · Thea, in Part VI, Ch. 7

text: In the course of twenty crowded years one parts with many illusions. I did not wish to lose the early ones. Some memories are realities, and are better than anything that can ever happen to one again.
author: Willa Cather
citation: My Antonia (1918) · Book V, Ch. 1

text: Whatever we had missed, we possessed together the precious, the incommunicable past.
author: Willa Cather
citation: My Antonia (1918) · Book V, Ch. 3

text: Where there is great love there are always miracles.
author: Willa Cather
citation: Death Comes for the Archbishop (1927) · Book I, Ch. 4

text: Elsewhere the sky is the roof of the world; but here the earth was the floor of the sky. The landscape one longed for when one was away, the thing all about one, the world one actually lived in, was the sky, the sky!
author: Willa Cather
citation: Death Comes for the Archbishop (1927) · Book VII, Ch. 4

text: One cannot divine nor forecast the conditions that will make happiness; one only stumbles upon them by chance, in a lucky hour, at the world’s end somewhere, and hold fast to the days, as to fortune or fame.
author: Willa Cather
citation: Willa Cather in Europe (1956) · Ch. 13 (10 September 1902)

text: Understanding is a two-way street.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: As quoted in Modern Quotations for Ready Reference (1947) by Arthur Richmond, p. 455

text: Life was meant to be lived, and curiosity must be kept alive. One must never, for whatever reason, turn his back on life.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: Preface (December 1960) to The Autobiography of Eleanor Roosevelt (1961), p. xix

text: I think, at a child’s birth, if a mother could ask a fairy godmother to endow it with the most useful gift, that gift should be curiosity.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: From article "In Defense of Curiosity" appearing in The Saturday Evening Post 208 (August 24, 1935); 8-9, 64-66.

text: I think that somehow, we learn who we really are and then live with that decision.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
work: Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time
citation: As quoted in Peter's Quotations : Ideas for Our Time (1972) by Laurence J. Peter, p. 5

text: Friendship with oneself is all-important, because without it one cannot be friends with anyone else in the world.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
work: The Beacon Book of Quotations by Women
citation: As quoted in The Beacon Book of Quotations by Women (1992) by Rosalie Maggio, p. 130

text: The most important thing in any relationship is not what you get but what you give.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: This Is My Story (1937)

text: One’s philosophy is not best expressed in words; it is expressed in the choices one makes.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: You Learn by Living (1960) · Foreword (January 1960)

text: One thing life has taught me: if you are interested, you never have to look for new interests. They come to you.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: You Learn by Living (1960) · p. 14

text: Happiness is not a goal, it is a by-product. Paradoxically, the one sure way not to be happy is deliberately to map out a way of life in which one would please oneself completely and exclusively.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: You Learn by Living (1960) · p. 95

text: It takes courage to love, but pain through love is the purifying fire which those who love generously know.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt

text: One of the blessings of age is to learn not to part on a note of sharpness, to treasure the moments spent with those we love, and to make them whenever possible good to remember, for time is short.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: My Day (1935–1962) · 5 February 1943

text: I have never felt that anything really mattered but the satisfaction of knowing that you stood for the things in which you believed and had done the very best you could.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: My Day (1935–1962) · 8 November 1944

text: There never has been security. No man has ever known what he would meet around the next corner; if life were predictable it would cease to be life, and be without flavor.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: Tomorrow Is Now (1963) · p. 80

text: In the long run there is no more exhilarating experience than to determine one’s position, state it bravely and then act boldly.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: Tomorrow Is Now (1963) · pp. 119–120

text: Example is the best lesson there is.
author: Eleanor Roosevelt
citation: Tomorrow Is Now (1963)

text: Not I, not I, but the wind that blows through me!
author: D. H. Lawrence
work: Song of a Man who has Come Through
citation: Song of a Man who has Come Through (1917)

text:
The tiny fish enjoy themselves
in the sea.
Quick little splinters of life,
their little lives are fun to them
in the sea.
author: D. H. Lawrence
citation: Little Fish (1929)

text:
Those that go searching for love
only make manifest their own lovelessness,
and the loveless never find love,
only the loving find love,
and they never have to seek for it.
author: D. H. Lawrence
work: The Works of D. H. Lawrence
citation: "Search for Love" in The Works of D. H. Lawrence, Wordsworth Editions, (1994), p. 552

text:
The gods are nameless and imageless
yet looking in a great full lime-tree of summer
I suddenly saw deep into the eyes of gods:
it is enough.
author: D. H. Lawrence
citation: More Pansies (1932) · "What Are The Gods?"

text: If we would build on a sure foundation in friendship, we must love friends for their sake rather than for our own.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Carolyn Warner (1992), page 135

text: I avoid looking forward or backward, and try to keep looking upward.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: 15 January, 1849. As quoted in Elizabeth Gaskell The life of Charlotte Brontë (1870), p. 285

text: Conventionality is not morality. Self-righteousness is not religion. To attack the first is not to assail the last.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Jane Eyre (1847) · Preface, 2nd edition (21 December 1847)

text: It is not violence that best overcomes hate — nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Jane Eyre (1847) · Helen Burns to Jane (Ch. 6)

text: If all the world hated you, and believed you wicked, while your own conscience approved you, and absolved you from guilt, you would not be without friends.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Jane Eyre (1847) · Helen Burns to Jane (Ch. 8)

text: It is in vain to say human beings ought to be satisfied with tranquility: they must have action; and they will make it if they cannot find it.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Jane Eyre (1847) · Jane (Ch. 12)

text: The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Jane Eyre (1847) · Jane (Ch. 27)

text: I have not much pride under such circumstances: I would always rather be happy than dignified.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Jane Eyre (1847) · Ch. 34

text: This is a terrible hour, but it is often that darkest point which precedes the rise of day; that turn of the year when the icy January wind carries over the waste at once the dirge of departing winter, and the prophecy of coming spring.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Shirley (1849) · Ch. 20: To-Morrow

text: I believe in some blending of hope and sunshine sweetening the worst lots. I believe that this life is not all; neither the beginning nor the end. I believe while I tremble; I trust while I weep.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: Villette (1853) · Chapter XXXI: The Dryad

text: Better to be without logic than without feeling.
author: Charlotte Brontë
citation: The Professor (1857) · Ch. XXIV

text:
However old, incapable,
And heart-sick I may be,
The moment I recall your face
My youth’s restored to me.
author: Hafez
work: I am a Bird from Paradise
citation: I am a Bird from Paradise, trans. Dick Davis (Penguin Classics)

text:
What holds in peace this two-fold world, let this two-fold sentence show
Amity to every friend, courtesy to every foe.
author: Hafez
citation: A Dictionary of Oriental Quotations (1911) · p. 19, Ode, 6 (Bicknell)

text:
Opportunity flies, O brother,
As the cloud that quick doth pass;
Oh make use of it! life is precious
If we let it go,—alas!
author: Hafez
citation: A Dictionary of Oriental Quotations (1911) · p. 34 (Bicknell)

text:
Come! hear of those who have felt sorrow’s touch
Their words are few, but what they mean is much.
author: Hafez
citation: A Dictionary of Oriental Quotations (1911) · p. 39, Ode 282 (Bicknell)

text:
How well said the aged farmer to his son,
O light of my eyes, thou wilt not reap save that which thou hast sown.
author: Hafez
citation: A Dictionary of Oriental Quotations (1911) · p. 67 (E. G. Browne)

text:
High birth may be a pearl of lustre, but let thine effort be
To rise by deeds. Distinct is greatness from birth and pedigree.
author: Hafez
citation: A Dictionary of Oriental Quotations (1911) · p. 99, Ode 104 (Bicknell)

text: The world would be a pretty dull place if it were made up only of the first-rate, right?
author: Haruki Murakami
citation: "Man-Eating Cats"

text: Even castles in the sky can do with a fresh coat of paint.
author: Haruki Murakami
work: South of the Border, West of the Sun
citation: South of the Border, West of the Sun

text: If your confusion leads you in the right direction, the results can be uncommonly rewarding.
author: Haruki Murakami
citation: Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World (1985) · Chapter One

text: You are not lost. It’s just that your own thoughts are being kept from you, or hidden away. But the mind is strong. It survives even without thought. Even with everything taken away, it holds a seed-your self. You must believe in your powers.
author: Haruki Murakami
citation: Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World (1985) · Chapter 24: Shadow Grounds

text: If you’re in pitch blackness, all you can do is sit tight until your eyes get used to the dark.
author: Haruki Murakami
citation: Norwegian Wood (1987)

text: I am for people. I can’t help it.
author: Charlie Chaplin
citation: As quoted in The Observer [London] (28 September 1952)

text: Life is a beautiful, magnificent thing, even to a jellyfish.
author: Charlie Chaplin
citation: Calvero's answer to Terry's question: "What is there to fight for?" in Limelight (1952)

text: Life is a tragedy when seen in close-up, but a comedy in long-shot.
author: Charlie Chaplin
citation: As quoted in his obituary in The Guardian (28 December 1977)

text: In this world, there is room for everyone. And the good earth is rich and can provide for everyone. The way of life can be free and beautiful, but we have lost the way.
author: Charlie Chaplin
citation: The Great Dictator (1940) · The Barber's speech

text:
There are two ways of spreading light: to be
The candle or the mirror that reflects it.
author: Edith Wharton
citation: "Vesalius in Zante (1564)", in North American Review (November 1902), p. 631

text: True originality consists not in a new manner but in a new vision.
author: Edith Wharton
citation: The Writing of Fiction (1925), ch. I

text: Life is always a tightrope or a feather bed. Give me the tightrope.
author: Edith Wharton
citation: Journal entry (March 1926)

text: Habit is necessary; it is the habit of having habits, of turning a trail into a rut, that must be incessantly fought against if one is to remain alive.
author: Edith Wharton
citation: A Backward Glance (1934) · "A First Word"

text: In spite of illness, in spite even of the archenemy sorrow, one can remain alive long past the usual date of disintegration if one is unafraid of change, insatiable in intellectual curiosity, interested in big things, and happy in small ways.
author: Edith Wharton
citation: A Backward Glance (1934) · "A First Word"

text: What after all, has maintained the human race on this old globe despite all the calamities of nature and all the tragic failings of mankind, if not faith in new possibilities, and courage to advocate them.
author: Jane Addams
work: Peace and Bread in Time of War
citation: Peace and Bread in Time of War (1922), Chapter 7 : Personal Reactions During War

text:
My heart is like a singing bird
Whose nest is in a water’d shoot;
My heart is like an apple-tree
Whose boughs are bent with thick-set fruit.
author: Christina Rossetti
citation: A Birthday, st. 1 (1861).

text:
For there is no friend like a sister
In calm or stormy weather;
To cheer one on the tedious way,
To fetch one if one goes astray,
To lift one if one totters down,
To strengthen whilst one stands.
author: Christina Rossetti
citation: Goblin Market, st. 28 (1862).

text:
Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads
The wind is passing by.
author: Christina Rossetti
citation: Who Has Seen the Wind?, st. 2 (1872).

text:
One day in the country
Is worth a month in town.
author: Christina Rossetti
citation: Summer; reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919).

author: Helen Hunt Jackson
citation: Verses (1874) · "Shadow of Birds", Stanza 2, p. 130

text:
The goldenrod is yellow;
The corn is turning brown:
The trees in apple orchards
With fruit are bending down.
author: Helen Hunt Jackson
citation: Poems (1892) · "September", Stanza 1, p. 206.

text:
When on the ground red apples lie
In piles like jewels shining,
And redder still on old stone walls
Are leaves of woodbines twining.
author: Helen Hunt Jackson
citation: Poems (1892) · "October's Bright Blue Weather", Stanza 4, p. 255.

text: ‘Crazy-busy’ is a great armor, it’s a great way for numbing. What a lot of us do is that we stay so busy, and so out in front of our life, that the truth of how we’re feeling and what we really need can’t catch up with us.
author: Brené Brown
citation: Washington Post, October 2012

text: Shame hates to have words wrapped around it. If we talk about it, it loses its grip on us.
author: Brené Brown
citation: University of Houston, Pride Stories

text: Avoidance will make you feel less vulnerable in the short run, but it will never make you less afraid.
author: Brené Brown
citation: Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience (2021)

text: Vulnerability is not weakness; it’s our greatest measure of courage.
author: Brené Brown
citation: Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience (2021)

text: Just as healing physical pain requires describing it, talking about it, and sometimes getting professional help, we need to do the same thing with emotional pain.
author: Brené Brown
citation: Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience (2021)

text: We have to belong to ourselves as much as we need to belong to others. Any belonging that asks us to betray ourselves is not true belonging.
author: Brené Brown
citation: Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience (2021)

text: We are called to assist the Earth to heal her wounds and in the process heal our own—indeed, to embrace the whole creation in all its diversity, beauty, and wonder.
author: Wangari Maathai
citation: Her memoir, Unbowed: A Memoir (2006).

text: No matter how dark the cloud, there is always a thin, silver lining, and that is what we must look for. The silver lining will come, if not to us then to next generation or the generation after that. And maybe with that generation the lining will no longer be thin.
author: Wangari Maathai
citation: Wangari Maathai quotes from Goodreads

text: When I was five, I am told, and asked what my favorite things in the world were, I answered, “smoked salmon and Bach.” (Now, sixty years later, my answer would be the same.)
author: Oliver Sacks
citation: Uncle Tungsten (2001) · p. 182

text: It is better to be making the news than taking it; to be an actor rather than a critic.
author: Winston Churchill
work: The Story of the Malakand Field Force
citation: Early career (1897–1929) · The Story of the Malakand Field Force (1898), Chapter VIII

text: What is the use of living, if it be not to strive for noble causes and to make this muddled world a better place for those who will live in it after we are gone?
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Early career (1897–1929) · Speech at Kinnaird Hall, Dundee, Scotland ("Unemployment"), October 10, 1908, in Liberalism and the Social Problem (1909), Churchill, Echo Library (2007), p. 87

text: We are going on swinging bravely forward along the grand high road and already behind the distant mountains is the promise of the sun.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Early career (1897–1929) · Speech at Kinnaird Hall, Dundee, Scotland ("Unemployment"), October 10, 1908, in Liberalism and the Social Problem (1909), Churchill, Echo Library (2007), p. 87

text: To improve is to change, so to be perfect is to have changed often.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Early career (1897–1929) · During a debate with Philip Snowden, 1st Viscount Snowden (June 23, 1925); Complete Speeches, 1897–1963, edited by Robert Rhodes James, Chelsea House ed., vol. 4 (1922–1928), p. 3706 · Often misquoted as: "To improve is to change, to be perfect is to change often."

text: Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities, because, as has been said, it is the quality which guarantees all others.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: 1930-1935 Wilderness Years · In an article published in “Collier’s” magazine about King Alfonso XIII of Spain on 27 June 1931. Source: 1931 June 27, Collier’s, Unlucky Alfonso by Winston Churchill, Start Page 11, Quote Page 49, Column 2, P. F. Collier and Son, New York. (Unz Database). As quoted in: Quote Investigator (July 14, 2019): Courage Is Rightly Esteemed the First of Human Qualities Because . . . It Is the Quality Which Guarantees All Others. Archived from the original on July 7, 2023.

text: I never “worry” about action, but only about inaction.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: The Second World War (1939–1945) · 1941 · Reported in Richard Langworth, ed., Churchill by Himself: The Definitive Collection of Quotations (New York: PublicAffairs, 2008), p. 160. · See also: 1940s. Passim. Martin Gilbert, The Churchill War Papers, Volume II: Never Surrender, May 1940–December 1940 (London: Heinemann; New York: Norton, 1994), p. xvi, where Sir Martin writes in his Preface: "Inefficiency, incompetence and negative attitudes roused his ire: I have indicated some examples of this in the Churchill index entry, under "rebukes by." He did not take kindly to what he called "a drizzle of carping criticism," or to those officials, military or civilian, who, as he expressed it, "failed to rise to the height of circumstances." Among his injunctions to his Ministers were, "Don't let this matter sleep," and, "I never 'worry' about action, but only about inaction."" · See also: In a letter, on page 1184 of the above work: Concerning "Operation Compass," the first major British offensive in North Africa, Churchill wrote to General Dill on 7 December 1940: "If, with the situation as it is, General Wavell is only playing small, and is not hurling on his whole available forces with furious energy, he will have failed to rise to the height of circumstances. I never "worry" about action, but only about inaction." · Source for all the aforementioned information: Richard M. Langworth (Senior fellow, Hillsdale College Churchill Project, Writer and Historian), Churchill on Action vs. Inaction (4 March 2009); Archived on June 2, 2020 and secured on June 2, 2020 from the original.

text: Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: The Second World War (1939–1945) · 1942 · Speech at Lord Mayor's Luncheon, Mansion House, London (10 November 1942) (partial text) · Referring to the British victory over the German Afrika Korps at the Second Battle of El Alamein in Egypt.

text: The empires of the future are the empires of the mind.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: The Second World War (1939–1945) · 1943 · Speech at Harvard University, September 6, 1943 (full text, audio).

text: The longer you can look back, the farther you can look forward.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: The Second World War (1939–1945) · 1944 · 2 March 1944, Speech to the Royal College of Physicians, London. Quoted in Churchill by Himself (2008), ed. Langworth, PublicAffairs, p. 25 · Often misquoted, see section "Misattributed" below

text: It is a mistake to look too far ahead. Only one link in the chain of destiny can be handled at a time.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: The Second World War (1939–1945) · 1945 · Speech in the House of Commons, February 27, 1945 "Crimea Conference"; in The Second World War, Volume VI: Triumph and Tragedy (1954), Chapter XXIII – Yalta: Finale.

text: I am fond of pigs. Dogs look up to us. Cats look down on us. Pigs treat us as equals.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Post-war years (1945–1955) · Christopher Soames, speech at the Reform Club (28 April 1981), reported in Martin S. Gilbert, Winston S. Churchill. Volume Eight: Never Despair: 1945–1965. p. 304

text: All the greatest things are simple, and many can be expressed in a single word: Freedom; Justice; Honour; Duty; Mercy; Hope.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Post-war years (1945–1955) · United Europe Meeting, Albert Hall, London (May 14, 1947). Cited in Churchill by Himself, ed. Langworth, PublicAffairs (2008), p. 26

text: For myself I am an optimist — it does not seem to be much use being anything else.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Post-war years (1945–1955) · Lord Mayor's Banquet, Guildhall, London (9 November 1954) The Unwritten Alliance, page 195, Columbia University, NY (1966),page 195,

text: We are all worms. But I do believe I am a glow-worm.
author: Winston Churchill
work: Winston Churchill as I Knew Him
citation: Post-war years (1945–1955) · As quoted by Violet Bonham-Carter in Winston Churchill as I Knew Him (1965), according to The Yale Book of Quotations (2006), Fred R. Shapiro, Yale University Press, p. 155

text: We are masters of the unsaid words, but slaves of those we let slip out.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Post-war years (1945–1955) · Quoted in Words of Wisdom: Winston Churchill, Students' Academy, Lulu Press (2014), Section Three :

text: In the course of my life I have often had to eat my words, and I must confess that I have always found it a wholesome diet.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: Post-war years (1945–1955) · Quoted by Lord Normanbrook in Action This Day: Working With Churchill. Memoirs by Lord Norman Brook (And Others) (1968) · Often misquoted as: Eating my words has never given me indigestion..

text: When I look back on all these worries I remember the story of the old man who said on his deathbed that he had had a lot of trouble in his life, most of which had never happened.
author: Winston Churchill
citation: The Second World War (book series) (1948–1953) · The Second World War, Volume II: Their Finest Hour (1949) Chapter 8 (September Tensions)

text: You see how few things you have to do to live a satisfying and reverent life? If you can manage this, that’s all even the gods can ask of you.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book II · Thou seest how few be the things, the which if a man has at his command his life flows gently on and is divine. · II, 5 · Hays translation

text: Remember that all is opinion.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book II · Ὅτι πᾶν ὑπόληψις. · II, 15

text: A man should be upright, not kept upright.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book III · III, 5

text: By a tranquil mind I mean nothing else than a mind well ordered.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 3

text: People try to get away from it all—to the country, to the beach, to the mountains. You always wish that you could too. Which is idiotic: you can get away from it anytime you like. By going within. Nowhere you can go is more peaceful—more free of interruptions—than your own soul.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 4 · Hays translation

text: Choose not to be harmed—and you won’t feel harmed. Don’t feel harmed—and you haven’t been.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 7 · Hays translation

text: Ask yourself at every moment, “Is this necessary?”
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 24

text: You’re better off not giving the small things more time than they deserve.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 32 · Hays translation

text: Observe always that everything is the result of a change, and get used to thinking that there is nothing Nature loves so well as to change existing forms and to make new ones like them.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 36

text: Time is a sort of river of passing events, and strong is its current; no sooner is a thing brought to sight than it is swept by and another takes its place, and this too will be swept away.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 43

text: All that happens is as usual and familiar as the rose in spring and the crop in summer.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 44

text: To be like the rock that the waves keep crashing over. It stands unmoved and the raging of the sea falls still around it.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 49

text: It’s unfortunate that this has happened. No. It’s fortunate that this has happened and I’ve remained unharmed by it—not shattered by the present or frightened of the future. It could have happened to anyone. But not everyone could have remained unharmed by it.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 49a

text: So remember this principle when something threatens to cause you pain: the thing itself was no misfortune at all; to endure it and prevail is great good fortune.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IV · IV, 49a

text: The things you think about determine the quality of your mind. Your soul takes on the color of your thoughts.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book V · The soul becomes dyed with the colour of its thoughts. · V, 16 · Hays translation

text: Nothing happens to anyone that he can’t endure.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book V · Nothing happens to anybody which he is not fitted by nature to bear. · Οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ συμβαίνει ὃ οὐχὶ ἐκεῖνο πέφυκε φέρειν. · V, 18 · Hays translation

text: But true good fortune is what you make for yourself. Good fortune: good character, good intentions, and good actions.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book V · V, 37 · Hays translation

text: I do what is mine to do; the rest doesn’t disturb me.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VI · VI, 22 · Hays translation

text: The only thing that isn’t worthless: to live this life out truthfully and rightly. And be patient with those who don’t.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VI · VI, 47 · Hays translation

text: What is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VI · VI, 54

text: I can control my thoughts as necessary; then how can I be troubled?
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VII · VII, 2 · Hays translation

text: Never let the future disturb you. You will meet it, if you have to, with the same weapons of reason which today arm you against the present.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VII · VII, 8 (Penguin Classics edition of Meditations, translated by Maxwell Staniforth)

text: If you are distressed by anything external, the pain is not due to the thing itself, but to your estimate of it; and this you have the power to revoke at any moment.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VII · VII, 11.

text: Is any man afraid of change? Why what can take place without change?
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VII · VII, 18

text: Look within. Within is the fountain of the good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VII · VII, 59

text: Very little is needed to make a happy life.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VII · ἐν ὀλιγίστοις κεῖται τὸ εὐδαιμόνως βιῶσαι · VII, 67

text: The cucumber is bitter? Then throw it out. There are brambles in the path? Then go around them. That’s all you need to know.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VIII · VIII, 50 · Hays translation

text: No carelessness in your actions. No confusion in your words. No imprecision in your thoughts.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VIII · Be not careless in deeds, nor confused in words, nor rambling in thought. · VIII, 51 · Hays translation

text: A man standing by a spring of clear, sweet water and cursing it. While the fresh water keeps on bubbling up. He can shovel mud into it, or dung, and the stream will carry it away, wash itself clean, remain unstained.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VIII · VIII, 51 · Hays translation

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book VIII · All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them. (trans. Meric Casaubon). · Οἱ ἄνθρωποι γεγόνασιν ἀλλήλων ἕνεκεν· ἢ δίδασκε οὖν ἢ φέρε. · Long translation

text: Objective judgment, now, at this very moment. Unselfish action, now, at this very moment. Willing acceptance—now, at this very moment—of all external events. That’s all you need.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IX · IX, 6 · Hays translation

text: Today I escaped from anxiety. Or no, I discarded it, because it was within me, in my own perceptions—not outside.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book IX · IX, 13 · Hays translation

text: Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book X · Μηκέθ᾽ ὅλως περὶ τοῦ οἷόν τινα εἶναι τὸν ἀγαθὸν ἄνδρα διαλέγεσθαι, ἀλλὰ εἶναι τοιοῦτον. · X, 16

text: To live your brief life rightly, isn’t that enough?
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book X · X, 31 · Hays translation

text: Someone despises me. That’s their problem. Mine: not to do or say anything despicable. Someone hates me. Their problem. Mine: to be patient and cheerful with everyone, including them.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book XI · XI, 13 · Hays translation

text: How much more damage anger and grief do than the things that cause them.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book XI · XI, 18 · Hays translation

text: Consider that everything is opinion, and opinion is in thy power. Take away then, when thou choosest, thy opinion, and like a mariner, who has doubled the promontory, thou wilt find calm, everything stable, and a waveless bay.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Book XII · XII, 22

text: Not to feel exasperated or defeated or despondent because your days aren’t packed with wise and moral actions. But to get back up when you fail, to celebrate behaving like a human—however imperfectly—and fully embrace the pursuit you’ve embarked on.
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Quotes from different translations · V. 9, trans. Gregory Hays

text: Does the light of a lamp shine and keep its glow until its fuel is spent? Why shouldn’t your truth, justice, and self-control shine until you are extinguished?
author: Marcus Aurelius
citation: Meditations (c. AD 121–180) · Quotes from different translations · XII. 15

text: Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: Repeated throughout his life (with variants); see: Quote Investigator

text: I am enough of an artist to draw freely upon my imagination. Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1920s · Viereck interview (1929)

text: I believe in standardizing automobiles. I do not believe in standardizing human beings.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1920s · Viereck interview (1929)

text: Life is like riding a bicycle. To keep your balance you must keep moving.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1930s · Letter to his son Eduard (5 February 1930), as quoted in Walter Isaacson, Einstein: His Life and Universe (2007), p. 367

text: I never think of the future. It comes soon enough.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1930s · Attributed in The Encarta Book of Quotations to an interview on the Belgenland (December 1930), which was the ship on which he arrived in New York that month. According to The Ultimate Quotable Einstein by Alice Calaprice (2010), p. 18, the quote also appears as "Aphorism, 1945-1946" in the Einstein Archives 36-570. Calaprice speculates that "perhaps it was recalled later and inserted into the archives under the later date." According to a snippet on Google Books, the phrase '"I never think of the future," he said. "It comes soon enough."' appears in The Literary Digest: Volume 107 on p. 29, in an article titled "We May Not 'Get' Relativity, But We Like Einstein" from 27 December 1930. The snippet also discusses the "welcome to Professor Einstein on the Belgenland" in New York

text: Only a life lived for others is a life worthwhile.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1930s · In answer to a question asked by the editors of Youth, a journal of Young Israel of Williamsburg, NY. Quoted in the New York Times (June 20, 1932), p. 17 · Unsourced variant: Only a life in the service of others is worth living.

text: Although I am a typical loner in daily life, my consciousness of belonging to the invisible community of those who strive for truth, beauty, and justice keeps me from feeling isolated.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1930s · My Credo (1932)

text: Do not worry about your difficulties in Mathematics. I can assure you mine are still greater.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1940s · Letter to high school student Barbara Lee Wilson (7 January 1943), Einstein Archives 42-606

text: Why is it nobody understands me and everybody likes me?
author: Albert Einstein
work: Everyone likes me, yet nobody understands me
citation: 1940s · As quoted in New York Times article "The Einstein Theory of Living; At 65 he leads the simplest of lives — and grapples with the most complex thoughts." (12 March 1944) · Variants: · Why is it that nobody understands me, yet everybody likes me? · Everyone likes me, yet nobody understands me.

text: One thing I have learned in a long life: that all our science, measured against reality, is primitive and childlike—and yet it is the most precious thing we have.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1950s · Letter to Hans Muehsam (9 July 1951), Einstein Archives 38-408, quoted in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein (2010) by Alice Calaprice, p. 404

text: The important thing is not to stop questioning.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1950s · Death of a Genius," LIFE magazine (2 May 1955) statement to William Miller, p. 64.

text: Try to become not a man of success, but try rather to become a man of value.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1950s · As quoted by LIFE magazine (2 May 1955)

text: I live in that solitude which is painful in youth, but delicious in the years of maturity.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1950s · Out of My Later Years (1950) · Ch. 2 "Self-Portrait" (1936), p. 5

text: Hail to the man who went through life always helping others, knowing no fear, and to whom aggressiveness and resentment are alien. Such is the stuff of which the great moral leaders are made.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1950s · Essay to Leo Baeck (1953) · The New Quotable Einstein

text: Joy in looking and comprehending is nature’s most beautiful gift.
author: Albert Einstein
citation: 1950s · Essay to Leo Baeck (1953) · Ideas and Opinions

text:
Nothing in the world is single,
All things by a law divine
In one spirit meet and mingle —
Why not I with thine?
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: "Love's Philosophy" (1819), st. 1

text:
The desire of the moth for the star,
Of the night for the morrow,
The devotion to something afar
From the sphere of our sorrow.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
work: One Word is Too Often Profaned
citation: One Word is Too Often Profaned (1821), st. 2

text:
Sing again, with your dear voice revealing
A tone
Of some world far from ours,
Where music and moonlight and feeling
Are one.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
work: To Jane. The keen Stars were twinkling
citation: To Jane. The keen Stars were twinkling; reported in Bartlett's Familiar Quotations, 10th ed. (1919)

text: Fear not the future, weep not for the past.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: The Revolt of Islam (1817) · Canto XI, st. 18

text:
I love all waste
And solitary places; where we taste
The pleasure of believing what we see
Is boundless, as we wish our souls to be.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: Julian and Maddalo (1819) · l. 14

text:
Be through my lips to unawaken’d earth
The trumpet of a prophecy! O Wind,
If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: Ode to the West Wind (1819) · St. V

author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: The Cloud (1820) · St. 7

text:
Hail to thee, blithe Spirit!
Bird thou never wert,
That from Heaven, or near it,
Pourest thy full heart
In profuse strains of unpremeditated art.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: To a Skylark (1821) · St. 1

text:
We look before and after,
And pine for what is not:
Our sincerest laughter
With some pain is fraught;
Our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: To a Skylark (1821) · St. 18

author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: Hellas (1821) · l. 34

text:
The world’s great age begins anew,
The golden years return,
The earth doth like a snake renew
Her winter weeds outworn;
Heaven smiles, and faiths and empires gleam,
Like wrecks of a dissolving dream.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

text:
I love tranquil solitude,
And such society
As is quiet, wise, and good;
Between thee and me
What difference? but thou dost possess
The things I seek, not love them less.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: Song: Rarely, Rarely, Comest Thou (1821) · St. 7

text: Poetry lifts the veil from the hidden beauty of the world, and makes familiar objects be as if they were not familiar.
author: Percy Bysshe Shelley
citation: A Defence of Poetry (1821)

text: Poetry is the record of the best and happiest moments of the happiest and best minds.

author: Audre Lorde

author: Audrey Hepburn
citation: Audrey Hepburn (2002) · p. 108

text:
The fog comes
on little cat feet.
It sits looking
over the harbor and city
on silent haunches, and then moves on.

Under the summer roses
When the flagrant crimson
Lurks in the dusk
Of the wild red leaves,
Love, with little hands,
Comes and touches you
With a thousand memories,
And asks you
Beautiful, unanswerable questions.

They wear long boots, hard boots.
author: Carl Sandburg

So many gods, so many creeds;
So many paths that wind and wind,
While just the art of being kind
Is all the sad world needs.

You never can tell when you do an act
Just what the result will be;
But with every deed you are sowing a seed,
Though the harvest you may not see.
author: Ella Wheeler Wilcox

Than darkness in the world; mine eyes are quick
To catch the first dim radiance of the dawn,
And slow to note the cloud that threatens storm.

Well worth the price of anguish. I detect
More good than evil in humanity.
Love lights more fires than hate extinguishes,
And men grow better as the world grows old.
author: Ella Wheeler Wilcox
citation: Poetry quotes · Poems of Pleasure (1900) · Optimism

Must nerve himself through valleys of despair.

All love that has not friendship for its base,
Is like a mansion built upon the sand.

Is the word that comes from the heart.
author: Ella Wheeler Wilcox

The firm resolve of a determined soul.

Is wholesome even for the King.

Are you – Nobody – Too?

If I can stop one heart from breaking,
I shall not live in vain;
If I can ease one life the aching,
Or cool one pain,
Or help one fainting robin
Unto his nest again,
I shall not live in vain.

How public – like a Frog –
To tell one’s name – the livelong June –
To an admiring Bog!

A Wisdom, without Face, or Name,
A Peace, as Hemispheres at Home
And so the Night became.

Does not concern the bee;
A clover, any time, to him
Is aristocracy.
author: Emily Dickinson

Who has not found the heaven below
Will fail of it above.
God’s residence is next to mine,
His furniture is love.

author: Louisa May Alcott

author: Louisa May Alcott

author: Maya Angelou

text: You did in your twenties what you knew how to do, and when you knew better you did better. And you should not be judged for the person that you were, but for the person that you’re trying to be and the woman that you are now.
author: Maya Angelou

author: Maya Angelou

author: Maya Angelou

author: Maya Angelou

You may write me down in history
With your bitter, twisted lies,
You may trod me in the very dirt
But still, like dust, I’ll rise.

author: Maya Angelou

author: Maya Angelou
citation: Conversations with Maya Angelou (1989) · 1977

text:
We grow despite the
horror that we feed
upon our own
tomorrow.
We grow.
author: Maya Angelou

text: If we are bold, love strikes away the chains of fear from our souls.
author: Maya Angelou
citation: A Brave and Startling Truth (1995)

text:
We, unaccustomed to courage
exiles from delight
live coiled in shells of loneliness
until love leaves its high holy temple
and comes into our sight
to liberate us into life.
author: Maya Angelou
citation: A Brave and Startling Truth (1995)

text:
When we come to it
We must confess that we are the possible
We are the miraculous, the true wonders of this world
That is when, and only when
We come to it.
author: Maya Angelou
citation: A Brave and Startling Truth (1995)

author: Maya Angelou

author: Neil Gaiman

author: Neil Gaiman

text: The world doesn’t have to be like this. Things can be different.
author: Neil Gaiman

text: Fiction is the lie that tells the truth, after all.
author: Neil Gaiman

text: I lived in books more than I lived anywhere else.
author: Neil Gaiman

author: Neil Gaiman
work: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
citation: Book quotes · The Ocean at the End of the Lane (2013) · Chapter 6 (p. 77)

author: Neil Gaiman

text: Honestly, if you’re given the choice between Armageddon or tea, you don’t say “what kind of tea?”
author: Neil Gaiman
