text: We have an obligation to make things beautiful. Not to leave the world uglier than we found it, not to empty the oceans, not to leave our problems for the next generation.
author: Neil Gaiman
citation: Book quotes · Why our future depends on libraries, reading and daydreaming (2013)

text: Empathy is a tool for building people into groups, for allowing us to function as more than self-obsessed individuals.
author: Neil Gaiman
citation: Book quotes · Why our future depends on libraries, reading and daydreaming (2013)

text: Google can bring you back, you know, a hundred thousand answers. A librarian can bring you back the right one.
author: Neil Gaiman
citation: Book quotes · Oral quotation about Google and librarians

text: Discontent is a good thing: discontented people can modify and improve their worlds, leave them better, leave them different.
author: Neil Gaiman
citation: Book quotes · Why our future depends on libraries, reading and daydreaming (2013)

text: I liked myths. They weren’t adult stories and they weren’t children’s stories. They were better than that. They just were.
author: Neil Gaiman
work: The Ocean at the End of the Lane
citation: Book quotes · The Ocean at the End of the Lane (2013) · Chapter 6 (p. 69)

text: Writers may be solitary but they also tend to flock together: they like being solitary together.
author: Neil Gaiman
citation: 2002 · January magazine interview (2002)

text: Life imitates art, but clumsily, copying its movements when it thinks it isn’t looking.
author: Neil Gaiman
citation: Book quotes · Trigger Warning (2015) · Introduction to Feminine Endings (p. xxxvi)

text: Why do I have this imagination? It’s the only one I’ve got!
author: Neil Gaiman
citation: 2007 · San Diego Comicon (2007)

text: It is a little dark still, but there are warnings of the day and somewhere out of the darkness a bird is singing to the Dawn.
author: Paul Laurence Dunbar
citation: Representative American Negroes, an essay from The Negro Problem, a collection of essays written in 1903 by leading African Americans.

text:
An angel, robed in spotless white,
Bent down and kissed the sleeping Night.
Night woke to blush; the sprite was gone.
Men saw the blush and called it Dawn.
author: Paul Laurence Dunbar

text: Blest hour! it was a luxury — to be!
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: "Reflections on Having Left a Place of Retirement", l. 43 (1795)

text: In nature there is nothing melancholy.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: The Nightingale: A Conversation Poem, ll. 13-22 (1798)

text: Joy rises in me, like a summer’s morn.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: "A Christmas Carol", st. viii (1799)

text:
Tranquillity! thou better name
Than all the family of Fame!
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: "Ode to Tranquillity", st. 1 (1801)

text: My eyes make pictures, when they are shut.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: "A Day-Dream", l. 1 (1828)

author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: "Youth and Age", st. 2 (1823–1832)

text:
There is not wind enough to twirl
The one red leaf, the last of its clan,
That dances as often as dance it can,
Hanging so light, and hanging so high,
On the topmost twig that looks up at the sky.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: Christabel (wr. 1797–1801; pub. 1816) · Part I, l. 48

text:
O lady! we receive but what we give
And in our life alone does Nature live.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: Dejection: An Ode (1802) · St. 4

text: The Dwarf sees farther than the Giant, when he has the Giant’s shoulders to mount on.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: The Friend (1809–1810) · No. 15 (November 30, 1809), p. 228 · Cf. Isaac Newton, letter to Robert Hooke (15 February 1676): "If I have seen further it is only by standing on the shoulders of giants".

text:
All thoughts, all passions, all delights,
Whatever stirs this mortal frame,
All are but ministers of Love,
And feed his sacred flame.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge

text:
Old Friends burn dim, like lamps in noisome air,
Love them for what they are; nor love them less,
Because to thee they are not what they were.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: Duty surviving Self-Love (1826)

text:
Sea, and hill, and wood,
With all the numberless goings-on of life,
Inaudible as dreams!
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: "Frost at Midnight", l. 11 (1798)

text:
Joy is the sweet voice, Joy the luminous cloud —
We in ourselves rejoice!
And thence flows all that charms or ear or sight,
All melodies the echoes of that voice,
All colours a suffusion from that light.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: Dejection: An Ode (1802) · St. 5

text:
Often do the spirits
Of great events stride on before the events,
And in to-day already walks to-morrow.
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
citation: Wallenstein (1800) · Part II: The Death of Wallenstein, Act v, scene 1

text:
No one worth possessing
Can be quite possessed.
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Advice to a Girl, Strange Victory (1933)

text:
Oh, is it not enough to be
Here with this beauty over me?
My throat should ache with praise, and I
Should kneel in joy beneath the sky.
Oh, beauty are you not enough?
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Rivers to the Sea (1915) · "Spring Night"

text:
Life has loveliness to sell,
All beautiful and splendid things,
Blue waves whitened on a cliff,
Soaring fire that sways and sings,
And children’s faces looking up
Holding wonder like a cup.
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Love Songs (1917) · "Barter"

text:
Spend all you have for loveliness,
Buy it and never count the cost;
For one white singing hour of peace
Count many a year of strife well lost,
And for a breath of ecstasy
Give all you have been, or could be.
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Love Songs (1917) · "Barter"

text:
O lovely chance, what can I do
To give my gratefulness to you?
You rise between myself and me
With a wise persistency;
I would have broken body and soul,
But by your grace, still I am whole.
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Flame and Shadow (1920) · "Lovely Chance"

text:
The window-lights, myriads and myriads,
Bloom from the walls like climbing flowers.
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Flame and Shadow (1920) · "Evening: New York"

text:
If I am peaceful, I shall see
Beauty’s face continually;
Feeding on her wine and bread
I shall be wholly comforted,
For she can make one day for me
Rich as my lost eternity.
author: Sara Teasdale
citation: Flame and Shadow (1920) · "The Wind in the Hemlock"

text:
I would live in your love as the sea-grasses live in the sea,
Borne up by each wave as it passes, drawn down by each wave that recedes.
author: Sara Teasdale
work: Helen of Troy and Other Poems
citation: Helen of Troy and Other Poems (1911) · "I Would Live in Your Love"

text:
I’d rather be my honest self
Than any made-up daisy.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
citation: "Discontent", in St. Nicholas Magazine, Vol. 3 (February 1876), p. 247

text:
Look bravely up into the sky,
And be content with knowing
That God wished for a buttercup
Just here, where you are growing.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
citation: "Discontent", in St. Nicholas Magazine, Vol. 3 (February 1876), p. 247

text: A harbor, even if it is a little harbor, is a good thing, since adventurers come into it as well as go out, and the life in it grows strong, because it takes something from the world, and has something to give in return.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
citation: Country By-Ways, River Driftwood (1881)

text:
Your patience may have long to wait,
Whether in little things or great,
But all good luck, you soon will learn,
Must come to those who nobly earn.
Who hunts the hay-field over
Will find the four-leaved clover.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
citation: "Perseverance" in St. Nicholas Magazine, Vol. X. (September 1883), p. 840

text: ‘Tain’t worthwhile to wear a day all out before it comes.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
work: The Country of the Pointed Firs
citation: The Country of the Pointed Firs (1896) · Ch. 16

text: The road was new to me, as roads always are, going back.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
work: The Country of the Pointed Firs
citation: The Country of the Pointed Firs (1896) · Ch. 19

text: Yes’m, old friends is always best, ‘less you can catch a new one that’s fit to make an old one out of.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
work: The Country of the Pointed Firs
citation: The Country of the Pointed Firs (1896) · Ch. 12

text: Tact is after all a kind of mind-reading.
author: Sarah Orne Jewett
work: The Country of the Pointed Firs
citation: The Country of the Pointed Firs (1896) · Ch. 10

text: There must be quite a few things a hot bath won’t cure, but I don’t know many of them.
author: Sylvia Plath
citation: The Bell Jar (1963) · Ch. 2

text: I never feel so much myself as when I’m in a hot bath.
author: Sylvia Plath
citation: The Bell Jar (1963) · Ch. 2

text: I took a deep breath and listened to the old brag of my heart: I am, I am, I am.
author: Sylvia Plath
citation: The Bell Jar (1963) · Ch. 20

text:
I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead;
I lift my lids and all is born again.
author: Sylvia Plath
citation: "Mad Girl's Love Song" (1953) from Collected Poems (1981)

text: The only man who makes no mistakes is the man who never does anything.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1900s · As quoted by Jacob A. Riis in Theodore Roosevelt, the Citizen (1904), chapter XVI A Young Men's Hero

text: It is hard to fail, but it is worse never to have tried to succeed. In this life we get nothing save by effort. Freedom from effort in the present merely means that there has been stored up effort in the past.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
work: The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses
citation: 1900s · The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses (1900) · The Strenuous Life

text: Far better it is to dare mighty things, to win glorious triumphs, even though checkered by failure, than to rank with those poor spirits who neither enjoy much nor suffer much, because they live in that grey twilight that knows neither victory nor defeat.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
work: The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses
citation: 1900s · The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses (1900) · The Strenuous Life

text: We cannot avoid meeting great issues. All that we can determine for ourselves is whether we shall meet them well or ill.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
work: The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses
citation: 1900s · The Strenuous Life: Essays and Addresses (1900) · The Strenuous Life

text: I have never in my life envied a human being who led an easy life; I have envied a great many people who led difficult lives and led them well.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1910s · Address in Des Moines, Iowa (4 November 1910)

text: When the weather is good for crops it is also good for weeds.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1900s · Address at Providence (1901)

text: There were all kinds of things I was afraid of at first, ranging from grizzly bears to ‘mean’ horses and gun-fighters; but by acting as if I was not afraid I gradually ceased to be afraid.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1910s · Theodore Roosevelt — An Autobiography (1913) · Chapter II The Vigor of Life

text: There are many kinds of success in life worth having.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1910s · Theodore Roosevelt — An Autobiography (1913) · Ch. IX : Outdoors and Indoors, p. 336; the final statement "quoted by Squire Bill Widener" as well as variants of it, are often misattributed to Roosevelt himself. · Variant: Do what you can, with what you have, where you are.

text: I have already lived and enjoyed as much life as any nine other men I have known.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1910s · As quoted in "Roosevelt The Greatest Outdoor Man" by Arthur K. Willyoung in Outing Vol. 74, No. 6 (September 1919), p. 353

text: Our words must be judged by our deeds; and in striving for a lofty ideal we must use practical methods; and if we cannot attain all at one leap, we must advance towards it step by step, reasonably content so long as we do actually make some progress in the right direction.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1910s · Nobel lecture (1910)

text: Success does not lie entirely in the hands of any one of us.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1900s · Address at the Prize Day Exercises at Groton School (1904)

text: A sound body is good; a sound mind is better; but a strong and clean character is better than either.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1900s · Address at the Prize Day Exercises at Groton School (1904)

text: The two feelings, envy and arrogance, are but opposite sides of the same shield, but different developments of the same spirit.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1900s · A Square Deal (1903)

text: From the greatest to the smallest, happiness and usefulness are largely found in the same soul, and the joy of life is won in its deepest and truest sense only by those who have not shirked life’s burdens.
author: Theodore Roosevelt
citation: 1900s · A Square Deal (1903)

text: To love or to have loved, that is enough. Ask nothing further. There is no other pearl to be found in the dark folds of life. To love is a consummation.
author: Victor Hugo
citation: Les Misérables (1862), page 1190, as translated by Charles Wilbour and provided by A.L. Bert Publishers. Source: Shawn Thomas (June 24, 2013): Quotes & Illustrations From Victor Hugo’s Les Miserables. Archived from the original on March 11, 2023.

text: Change your opinions, keep to your principles; change your leaves, keep intact your roots.
author: Victor Hugo
citation: "Thoughts," Postscriptum de ma vie, in Victor Hugo's Intellectual Autobiography, Funk and Wagnalls (1907) as translated by Lorenzo O'Rourke

text: To divinise is human, to humanise is divine.
author: Victor Hugo
citation: Les feuilles d'automne (1831)

text:
I come into the presence of still water.
And I feel above me the day-blind stars
waiting with their light. For a time
I rest in the grace of the world, and am free.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: "The Peace of Wild Things" in Green River Review, No. 1 (1968)

text: The teachers are everywhere. What is wanted is a learner.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: What Are People For? (1990) · "Healing"

text: The context of love is the world.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: What Are People For? (1990) · "The Responsibility of the Poet"

text: I believe that the world was created and approved by love, that it subsists, coheres, and endures by love, and that, insofar as it is redeemable, it can be redeemed only by love.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Another Turn of the Crank (1996) · "Health is Membership"

text: Never forget: We are alive within mysteries.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Life Is A Miracle : An Essay Against Modern Superstition (2000)

text: We have more than we can know. We know more than we can say.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Life Is A Miracle : An Essay Against Modern Superstition (2000)

text:
Ask the world to reveal its quietude —
not the silence of machines when they are still,
but the true quiet by which birdsongs,
trees, bellworts, snails, clouds, storms
become what they are, and are nothing else.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Given (2005) · Sabbaths 2001

text:
Sit and be still
until in the time
of no rain you hear
beneath the dry wind’s
commotion in the trees
the sound of flowing
water among the rocks,
a stream unheard before,
and you are where
breathing is prayer.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Given (2005) · Sabbaths 2001

text:
Laugh.
Laughter is immeasurable. Be joyful
though you have considered all the facts.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Poems · "Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front" in Farming: A Hand Book (1970)

text: Love the world. Work for nothing.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Poems · "Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front" in Farming: A Hand Book (1970)

text: It is impossible to care for each other more or differently than we care for the earth.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: The Unsettling of America (1977), Chapter Seven : The Body and the Earth

text:
What I stand for
is what I stand on.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Poems · "Below" in A Part (1980)

text:
Ask the questions that have no answers.
Invest in the millenium.
author: Wendell Berry
citation: Poems · "Manifesto: The Mad Farmer Liberation Front" in Farming: A Hand Book (1970)

text: If a thing loves, it is infinite.
author: William Blake
citation: 1780s · Annotations to Swedenborg (1788)

text: If the doors of perception were cleansed, everything would appear to man as it is: infinite.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) · A Memorable Fancy

text: Eternity is in love with the productions of time.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) · Proverbs of Hell · Line 10

text: The busy bee has no time for sorrow.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) · Proverbs of Hell · Line 11

text: The hours of folly are measur’d by the clock, but of wisdom no clock can measure.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) · Proverbs of Hell · Line 12

text: The cistern contains: the fountain overflows.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) · Proverbs of Hell · Line 35

text: Think in the morning. Act in the noon. Eat in the evening. Sleep in the night.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) · Proverbs of Hell · Line 41

text:
To see a World in a Grain of Sand
And a Heaven in a Wild Flower,
Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand
And Eternity in an hour.
author: William Blake
citation: 1800s · Auguries of Innocence (1803) · Line 1

text:
Man was made for joy and woe,
And when this we rightly know
Through the world we safely go.
Joy and woe are woven fine,
A clothing for the soul divine.
author: William Blake
citation: 1800s · Auguries of Innocence (1803) · Line 56. Compare Psalm 30:5 (KJV): "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."

text:
Every tear from every eye
Becomes a babe in eternity.
author: William Blake
citation: 1800s · Auguries of Innocence (1803) · Line 67

text:
And throughout all eternity
I forgive you, you forgive me.
author: William Blake
citation: 1800s · Poems from Blake's Notebook (c. 1804) · My Specter, st. 14

text:
He who binds to himself a joy
Does the wingèd life destroy;
But he who kisses the joy as it flies
Lives in eternity’s sunrise.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · Poems from Blake's Notebook (c. 1791-1792) · Several Questions Answered · No. 1, He Who Binds

text:
I was angry with my friend:
I told my wrath, my wrath did end.
I was angry with my foe:
I told it not, my wrath did grow.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · Songs of Experience (1794) · A Poison Tree, st. 1

text:
Can I see another’s woe,
And not be in sorrow too?
Can I see another’s grief,
And not seek for kind relief?
author: William Blake
citation: 1780s · Songs of Innocence (1789–1790) · On Another's Sorrow, st. 1

text:
When the voices of children are heard on the green
And laughing is heard on the hill,
My heart is at rest within my breast
And everything else is still.
author: William Blake
citation: 1780s · Songs of Innocence (1789–1790) · Nurse's Song, st. 1

text:
The moon like a flower
In heaven’s high bower,
With silent delight,
Sits and smiles on the night.
author: William Blake
citation: 1780s · Songs of Innocence (1789–1790) · Night, st. 1

text:
Great things are done when men and mountains meet;
This is not done by jostling in the street.
author: William Blake
citation: 1800s · Poems from Blake's Notebook (c. 1807-1809) · Great Things Are Done

text: Fun I love, but too much Fun is of all things the most loathsom. Mirth is better than Fun & Happiness is better than Mirth.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · Letter to Revd. Dr. Trusler (1799)

text: This world of imagination is the world of eternity.
author: William Blake
work: A Vision of the Last Judgment
citation: 1810s · A Vision of the Last Judgment

text:
Love to faults is always blind,
Always is to joys inclined,
Lawless, winged, and unconfined,
And breaks all chains from every mind.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · Poems from Blake's Notebook (c. 1791-1792) · Love to Faults

text: Time is the mercy of Eternity; without Time’s swiftness Which is the swiftest of all things, all were eternal torment.
author: William Blake
citation: 1800s · Milton (c. 1809) · Book the First, 24:72

text: If the fool would persist in his folly he would become wise.
author: William Blake
citation: 1790s · The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (1790–1793) · Proverbs of Hell · Line 18

text:
The Angel that presided o’er my birth
Said, “Little creature, formed of joy and mirth,
Go love without the help of any thing on earth.”
author: William Blake
citation: 1800s · Poems from Blake's Notebook (c. 1807-1809) · The Angel That Presided

text: Don’t shortchange the future, because of fear in the present.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2009 · Barack Obama: "The President's News Conference With Prime Minister Gordon Brown of the United Kingdom in London, England," April 1, 2009. Online by Gerhard Peters and John T. Woolley, The American Presidency Project.

text: Human destiny will be what we make of it.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2009 · A World without Nuclear Weapons (April 2009)

text: We do not have to think that human nature is perfect for us to still believe that the human condition can be perfected. We do not have to live in an idealized world to still reach for those ideals that will make it a better place.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2009 · Nobel Prize acceptance speech (December 2009)

text: I believe we can be better.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2011 · Tucson Memorial Address (January 2011)

text: There’s only one thing we can be sure of, and that is the love that we have for our children, for our families, for each other. The warmth of a small child’s embrace, that is true.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2012 · Sandy Hook Prayer Vigil (December 2012)

text: Empathy is a quality of character that can change the world - one that makes you understand that your obligations to others extend beyond people who look like you and act like you and live in your neighborhood.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2006 · Commencement address at the University of Massachusetts Boston (June 2, 2006)

text:
The one rule that lies at the heart of every major religion is that we do unto others as we would have them do unto us.
Adhering to this law of love has always been the core struggle of human nature.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2009 · Nobel Prize acceptance speech (December 2009)

text: That’s where courage comes from — when we turn not from each other, or on each other, but towards one another, and we find that we do not walk alone. That’s where courage comes from.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2013 · "Let Freedom Ring" Ceremony (August 2013)

text: It’s the dreamers — no matter how humble or poor or seemingly powerless — that are able to change the course of human events.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2015 · Remarks at Panama Civil Society Forum (April 2015)

text: I’m still asking you to believe – not in my ability to bring about change, but in yours. I believe in change because I believe in you.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2017 · President Obama on Twitter at January 20, 2017; archived from the original on August 28, 2020. As quoted by ABC Radio (2017) and presented in the 2017-01-20 article "Obamas Offer Goodbye Message as They Leave the White House" by MyCentralOregon.com. Archived from the original and retrieved on August 28, 2020.

text: I don’t think it is inevitable that the world comes together in a common culture and common understanding. But overall, I am hopeful. And the reason I’m hopeful is, if you look at the trajectory of history, humanity has slowly improved.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2016 · Young Leaders of the Americas Initiative Town Hall (March 2016)

text: We are strongest when we see the inherent dignity in every human being.
author: Barack Obama
citation: 2015 · Address to the People of India (January 2015)
